en: May there be success for the virtuous in their goal through the grace of that Dhūrjaṭi,
upon whose head the digit of the moon rests like a streak of foam from the Ganges. (Hitopadeśa 0.1)
This *Hitopadeśa*, when heard, bestows proficiency in refined expressions,
versatility in speech everywhere, and the science of ethics.
Praise of Knowledge:
A wise person should contemplate knowledge and wealth as if they were free from old age and death;
yet, as if Death had seized him by the hair, he should practice the Dharma.
Among all material things, they say that knowledge alone is the unsurpassed wealth,
because it can never be stolen, it has no price, and it is forever inexhaustible.

Just as even a river flowing through low ground unites with the unassailable ocean, so too does learning unite even a man of humble origin with a king; beyond this, nothing is more powerful than destiny.
Knowledge bestows discipline; through discipline one attains worthiness;
from worthiness one acquires wealth; from wealth comes righteousness, and from that, happiness.
Knowledge is of two kinds for the sake of attainment: the science of weapons and the science of treatises.
The former leads to decline in old age, while the latter is always honored.
Just as an impression made upon a new vessel does not change otherwise, so too is moral conduct here taught to children under the guise of a story. (Hitopadeśa 0.8)
The acquisition of friends, the alienation of allies, war, and peace—these are written here, having been extracted from the *Pañcatantra* as well as other treatises. (Hitopadeśa 0.9)
Now, as for the introduction to the story: on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī there is a city named Pāṭaliputra.
There dwelt a king named Sudarśana, who was endowed with all the qualities of a sovereign lord.
Once that king heard two verses being recited by someone:
"The scripture which cuts through manifold doubts, reveals the imperceptible, and is the eye for all—he who does not possess it is truly blind. (Hitopadeśa 0.10)
Youth, wealth, power, and lack of discernment—each one by itself leads to ruin; how much more so when all four are present together?

Having heard this, the king, his mind distressed by the failure of his sons—who had not mastered the scriptures and were constantly following wrong paths—to practice those very scriptures, reflected: "What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous? What is the use of a one-eyed eye? It is merely a source of pain. (Hitopadeśa 0.12)
Among those who are unborn, dead, or foolish, the first two are better than the last;
for the first two cause suffering but once, while the last causes it at every step.
Moreover: Better is a miscarriage, better indeed is even not approaching [the womb], better is a dead child at birth, and better even is the birth of a daughter.
Better is a barren wife, and even better is dwelling in the womb,
than a son who is ignorant, even if he be endowed with beauty, wealth, and virtue.
He is truly born by whose birth a lineage attains greatness;
for in this revolving cycle of existence, who indeed does not die and not take birth again?
And furthermore:
He whose chalk-finger, in the flurry of beginning to enumerate the multitude of his virtues, does not falter;
Therefore, if a mother is one who has given birth to a son, tell me, what kind of woman is barren?
Moreover: He whose mind is not renowned for generosity, austerity, and valor,
nor for learning and the acquisition of wealth, is nothing but his mother’s excrement.
Furthermore:
Better is one virtuous son than even hundreds of fools;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas the hosts of stars cannot.
The son of one who has performed extremely difficult austerities at some sacred pilgrimage site shall be obedient, prosperous, righteous, and wise.
And so it has been said:

"Constant arrival of wealth, freedom from illness, a beloved wife who speaks kindly, an obedient son, and knowledge that brings profit—these six, O King, are the happinesses of the world of the living. (Hitopadeśa 0.20)
Who is truly fortunate by having many sons who merely fill granaries with measures of grain? Better is a single son who supports the lineage, through whom his father becomes renowned.
A father who incurs debt is an enemy; a mother who is unfaithful is an enemy;
a beautiful wife is an enemy; and an unlearned son is an enemy.
A man who possesses virtue is honored, regardless of his lineage;
what can even a bow do if it is devoid of string, despite being made from a pure bamboo?
Alas, alas, my son! These nights have passed without your studies;
therefore, you sink in the midst of the learned like a cow in the mud. (Hitopadeśa 0.24)
So, how now may these sons of mine be made virtuous? For:
"Eating, sleeping, fear, and sexual intercourse—these are common to men and beasts.
Knowledge is the superior distinction of men; those devoid of knowledge are equal to beasts. (Hitopadeśa 0.25)
For it is said:
"He for whom not even one among dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa exists, his birth is as useless as the teat on the neck of a goat. (Hitopadeśa 0.26)
And as it is said:
"Lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these five are indeed created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb. (Hitopadeśa 0.27)
Moreover:
"The events that are destined to happen occur even for the great:
the nakedness of the Blue-throated One (Śiva), and the reclining upon the great serpent of Hari (Viṣṇu). (Hitopadeśa 0.28)
Furthermore:
"That which was not to be will not be; and that which is to be cannot be otherwise.
Why is this medicine, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk? (Hitopadeśa 0.29)
This is the speech of certain people who are lazy and incapable of action.
It speaks of the excellence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*):
"For just as there can be no movement of a chariot with only one wheel,"
Likewise, without human effort, destiny does not succeed.
And thus:
"Action performed in a previous birth is called destiny;
therefore, one should exert effort through human endeavor without indolence. (Hitopadeśa 0.31)
One should not abandon one's own effort even after considering destiny;
for without effort, one cannot obtain oil from sesame seeds.
And furthermore:
Fortune attends the industrious lion among men; "it is to be given by fate," say the cowards.
Having overcome fate, exert human effort through your own power;
if success is not achieved despite the effort being made, what fault is there in this?
Just as a potter fashions from a lump of clay whatever he desires,
so does a human being experience the karma created by himself.

Even upon seeing a treasure-trove lying before him, as if by chance like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence, fate does not take it up itself; it depends upon human effort. For undertakings are accomplished through exertion, not by mere wishes.
For deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
And so it has been said:
"The mother is an enemy and the father is a foe by whom a child is not taught;
he does not shine in the midst of an assembly, like a crane in the midst of swans. (Hitopadeśa 0.37)
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of a noble lineage, do not shine if they are devoid of learning, like *kiṃśuka* flowers without fragrance. (Hitopadeśa 0.38)

Furthermore: That which has not been studied from books and has not been studied in the presence of a teacher does not shine in the midst of an assembly, like the pregnancy of a woman by a paramour. (Hitopadeśa 0.39)
Having reflected thus, the king convened an assembly of scholars.
The king said: "O scholars, listen to my words!"

Is there any such learned man who is capable of bringing about a second birth for my sons—who are constantly treading the wrong path and have not mastered the scriptures—by means of instruction in the science of ethics (*nīti-śāstra*)? For: "Glass, through contact with gold, acquires the luster of emeralds."
Likewise, through proximity to the virtuous, a fool attains proficiency.
And it has been said:
"For the intellect declines, dear son, through association with the inferior;
it reaches equality with equals, and excellence with the excellent. (Hitopadeśa 0.41)

In the meantime, a great scholar named Viṣṇuśarman, who was like Bṛhaspati and knew the true essence of all treatises on political ethics (*nīti*), said: "Your Majesty, these princes are born of a noble lineage; therefore, they can be made to grasp the principles of ethics by me. For it is said:
'No action, when placed in an unworthy recipient, can be fruitful.'"
Even with a hundred efforts, a crane cannot be made to speak like a parrot.
And furthermore:
In this lineage devoid of merit, no offspring of noble character is born; for how could a glass trinket be produced in a mine of precious gems? (Hitopadeśa 0.43)
"Therefore, within six months, I shall make your sons experts in the science of political ethics. The king replied with humility:
"Even a worm, through association with the fragrant flower, ascends to the heads of the virtuous."
Even a stone attains divinity when well-consecrated by the great.
And furthermore:
Just as a substance shines by its proximity to the mountain of sunrise, so too even one of lowly appearance shines through the presence of the virtuous. (Hitopadeśa 0.45)
Virtues remain virtues when found in those who recognize virtue; but upon encountering one devoid of virtue, they become faults. Rivers flow with water that is sweet to taste.
Having reached the ocean, they become accessible.
"Therefore, you are the authority for the instruction of these sons of mine in the science of polity," he said, and with great respect, he entrusted his sons into the hands of Viṣṇuśarman. —
Thus ends "The Acquisition of Friends."
Then, in the course of conversation before the princes who were seated comfortably on the roof of the palace, the wise man said: "O princes, listen!
For the intelligent, time passes in the diversion of poetry and the sciences;
but for fools, it passes in vice, sleep, or quarreling. (Hitopadeśa 1.1)
"Therefore, for your amusement, I shall tell you a wonderful tale concerning the crow, the tortoise, and others.
The princes said, "Noble sir,
let it be told!"
Viṣṇuśarman said: "Listen, all of you.
Now the acquisition of friends is being introduced, of which this is the first verse:"

Those who are intelligent and esteemed by their friends, though lacking means and destitute of wealth, quickly accomplish their tasks, just like the crow, the tortoise, the deer, and the mouse. (Hitopadeśa 1.2)
The princes asked, "How was that?
He replied: "On the bank of the Godāvarī there is a large śālmalī tree.
There, birds come from various regions and countries and dwell during the night."

Then once, when the night had declined and the blessed moon, the lord of the night-lilies, was hanging upon the crest of the western mountain, a crow named Laghupatana woke up and saw a tiger wandering like a second God of Death with a noose in its paw.
Beholding it, he thought: "This morning, an ill omen has appeared."

"I do not know what he will show that is undesirable," saying this, he moves about distractedly in the process of following after him; for: "There are thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for fear."
Day after day, they enter into the fool, but not the wise man.
Furthermore, this must necessarily be done by those who possess sense objects:
"Rising again and again, one should reflect: 'What good deed has been accomplished today?
For the sun will go to its setting, taking away a fragment of my life. (Hitopadeśa 1.4)
Then that hunter, having scattered grains of rice,
spread out his net and remained there concealed.
At that very moment, the king of pigeons named Citragrīva, traveling through the air with his retinue, observed the grains of rice.
Then the king of pigeons said to the pigeons who were greedy for the grains of rice: "How can there be a source of rice-grains here in this desolate forest?
Let this be investigated for a moment.
I do not see anything auspicious in this; for by this greed for rice-grains, we too will likely meet with the same fate."
But due to greed for a bracelet, a traveler sank into a most difficult mire and was killed by an old tiger. (Hitopadeśa 1.5)
The pigeons said: "How was that?
[The first] story:
He said, "Once, while wandering in the southern forest, I saw an old tiger who had bathed and held kusha grass in his paws, standing on the bank of a lake, saying: 'O travelers!'"
"Take this golden bracelet. Then, a certain traveler, drawn by greed, reflected: "This is possible through good fortune;
however, one should not act upon a matter involving doubt regarding oneself. For it is said:"
Even when one obtains what is desired from that which is undesired, no auspicious outcome arises;
for where there is contact with poison, even nectar leads to death. (Hitopadeśa 1.6)
However, there is indeed doubt regarding the pursuit of wealth in all circumstances;
as it has been said:
"Without embarking upon uncertainty, a man does not behold auspicious things."
But if, having again encountered doubt, he survives, he shall see [the truth].
I shall first investigate that.
He says aloud:
"Where is your bracelet?"
The tiger stretched out his paw and showed it to him.
The traveler said, "How can there be trust in you, whose very nature is that of a demon?
The tiger replied, "Listen, O traveler!"
In my youth, I was exceedingly wicked;
because of the slaughter of many cows and humans, my sons died and my wife passed away,
and I am now left without a lineage.
Then I was instructed by a certain righteous man:
"May you practice the duty of giving and other such virtues.
Because of that instruction and the like, I am now devoted to bathing, a donor, advanced in years, and with worn-out nails and teeth; how am I not a fit object for trust? And it has been said:
Sacrifice, study, giving, austerity, truthfulness, fortitude, forbearance,
and freedom from greed— this is remembered as the eightfold path of dharma.
Among these, the first group of four may be practiced even for the sake of hypocrisy;
however, the latter group of four resides only in the great-souled.

My freedom from greed is such that I wish to give even the golden bracelet on my own wrist to anyone at all; nevertheless, the public scandal that "a tiger is devouring a human" is difficult to avert. For it is said:
"The world follows the path of those who have gone before, like a woman following the advice of a procuress."
One does not accept as authoritative a person's teaching on Dharma, even if that person is a twice-born who has killed a cow.
I have also studied the treatises on dharma. Listen:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, just as rain in a desert wastes is like food to one oppressed by hunger, a gift given to a poor man bears fruit. (Hitopadeśa 1.11)
"As life is dear to oneself, so it is for all living beings;
therefore, the virtuous show compassion toward all beings by treating them as they would themselves. (Hitopadeśa 1.12)
Furthermore:
In refusing and in giving, in pleasure and pain, and in what is dear and what is not dear, a person attains the standard of judgment by means of comparison with oneself. (Hitopadeśa 1.13)
And furthermore:
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother, upon the wealth of others as a clod of earth, and upon all living beings as himself—he is a wise man. (Hitopadeśa 1.14)
And you are exceedingly destitute;
therefore, I am making an effort to give that to you.
And so it has been said:
Support the poor, O son of Kuntī; do not bestow wealth upon the wealthy.
Medicine is beneficial for one who is ill; what use is medicine to one who is healthy? (Hitopadeśa 1.15)
And furthermore:

That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who cannot return the favor, at the right place and time and to a worthy recipient—that gift they know to be *sāttvika*. (Hitopadeśa 1.16)
"Therefore, having bathed here in this lake, take this golden bracelet.
Then, as soon as he, believing those words, entered the lake out of greed to bathe, he sank into a great mire and was unable to escape.
Seeing him fallen into the mud, the tiger said, "Alas! You have fallen into great mud;
therefore, I shall lift you up.
Having said this, the tiger approached very slowly and seized the traveler, who thought to himself:
Neither the recitation of the Dharmaśāstras nor the study of the Vedas is the cause for a wicked person; rather,
it is their very nature that prevails in such a case.
Just as the milk of cows is sweet by its very nature.
Furthermore:
For those whose senses and minds are not under control, ritual action is like an elephant’s bath;
knowledge without action is like ornaments on an ugly person—it is merely a burden. (Hitopadeśa 1.18)
Therefore, I have acted wrongly in that I placed my trust here in one whose nature is Māra. And so it has been said:
One should never place trust in rivers, in those with weapons in hand, in clawed creatures, in horned animals, nor in women or royal families.
Furthermore:
For the intrinsic natures of all things are examined, and not their other qualities;
for intrinsic nature stands at the summit, transcending all qualities. (Hitopadeśa 1.20)
And furthermore:
He indeed dwells in the sky, the destroyer of impurities,
the bearer of a thousand rays, who moves in the midst of the luminaries.
Even the moon, by the turn of fate, is swallowed by Rāhu;
who is capable of erasing even what is written upon the forehead? (Hitopadeśa 1.21)
While he was thinking thus, he was seized by a tiger, killed, and devoured.
Therefore I say: "Out of greed for a bracelet," and so forth.
For this very reason, an action that has not been thoroughly deliberated upon must never be undertaken. As it is said:
Well-digested food, a wise son, a well-disciplined wife, a well-served king,
that which is spoken after careful reflection, and that which is done after thorough deliberation— these are the things that bring happiness.
Even over a very long period of time, it does not undergo transformation.
Having heard these words, a certain pigeon spoke with pride: "Ah! Why is it said thus?
For the word of an elder should be accepted when a time of calamity has arrived."
In this same manner, let one apply such investigation even toward food. (1.23)
For it is said:
"On this earth, every food and drink is beset by suspicions;
where, then, can activity be undertaken, or how indeed is one to live? (Hitopadeśa 1.24)
As it has been said:
"The envious, the censorious, the discontented, the angry, the ever-suspicious, and he who lives off the fortune of others—these six are constantly miserable. (Hitopadeśa 1.25)
Having heard this, all the pigeons descended from the vault of the sky out of greed for the grains of rice and settled there. For:
"Even those who are deeply learned and uphold the most extensive scriptures, though they are capable of resolving all doubts, suffer when deluded by greed. (Hitopadeśa 1.26)
Moreover: From greed arises anger; from greed desire is born;
from greed come delusion and destruction; greed is the cause of evil. (Hitopadeśa 1.27)
Furthermore:
The birth of a golden deer is impossible;
nevertheless, Rāma was lured by the deer.
Generally, when a time of calamity has arrived,
even the intellects of men become clouded.
Immediately thereafter, they all became entangled in a net;
then, they all began to revile him by whose word they had been suspended there. For it is said:
"One should not go at the head of a group, for when the task is accomplished, the fruit is shared equally."
If there should be a failure in the task, the talkative person therein is destroyed.
Hearing his reproach, Citragrīva said: "This is not his fault;
for when calamities descend, even a benefactor becomes a cause [of harm]. Indeed, the mother's own leg becomes a tethering post for the calf when it is bound. (Hitopadeśa 1.30)
And furthermore:
He alone is a kinsman who is capable of rescuing those who have fallen into calamity;
not one who is clever only at seizing material goods for the sake of protecting those already terrified. (Hitopadeśa 1.31)
In times of calamity, astonishment alone is the mark of a base man.
Therefore, relying here upon fortitude, let a remedy be considered; for—fortitude in adversity and forbearance in prosperity [are the marks of the great].
Eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle,
and a passion for fame— indeed, this addiction to sacred learning is innate to great souls. (Hitopadeśa 1.32)
The mother who gives birth to a son who feels no joy in prosperity, no dejection in adversity, and no cowardice in battle—she produces that rare ornament of the three worlds. (Hitopadeśa 1.33)
Furthermore: Six defects must be abandoned here by a man who desires prosperity:
sleep, lethargy, fear, anger, laziness, and procrastination. (Hitopadeśa 1.34)
Now, let it be done thus: let all of you, becoming one in mind, take up the net and fly away. For:
"Even of small things, a combination accomplishes the task;
by blades of grass that have attained the state of a rope, even rutting elephants are bound. (Hitopadeśa 1.35)
For men, even a union with those of their own family, however few, is better;
for rice grains abandoned even by a single husk do not sprout.
Having thus reflected, all the birds took up the net and flew away. Immediately thereafter, the hunter, seeing them carrying off the net from afar, ran after them and thought:
"United, these birds are carrying away my net."
But when they fall down, then they shall come under my control.
Then, when those birds had passed beyond the range of his vision, the hunter turned back.
Seeing that the hunter had departed, the pigeons said, "Master,
what is it now appropriate to do?"
Citragrīva said:
By their very nature, three—mother, friend, and father—are beneficial; others become well-wishers only through some purpose or motive. (Hitopadeśa 1.38)
"That friend of mine, the king of mice named Hiraṇyaka, dwells in the Citra forest on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī;
he will cut our snares," they reflected, and so they all went to the vicinity of Hiraṇyaka’s burrow.
Hiraṇyaka, however, always lived having made a burrow with a hundred openings out of fear of misfortune.
Then Hiraṇyaka, startled by the fear of the pigeons' descent, remained silent.
Citragrīva said, "Friend Hiraṇyaka,
why do you not speak with us?"
Then Hiraṇyaka, recognizing those words, went out in great haste and said: "Ah!
I am fortunate; my dear friend Citragrīva has arrived.
For one whose conversation is with a friend, and whose dwelling is with a friend—"
There is no one more meritorious in this world than he with whom a friend can converse.
Then, seeing them bound by nooses, he stood for a moment in astonishment and said, "Friend, what is this?
Citragrīva replied, "Friend,
this is the fruit of our actions in a previous birth."
Because of which, by which, in what manner, at what time, what,
how much, and where one's own karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is performed;
therefore, by that, in that manner, at that time, it is that [which results].
And for that long, and in that place, it comes about through the power of the Creator.
Passion, grief, torment, bondage, and misfortune—these are the fruits for embodied beings of the trees of their own transgressions. (Hitopadeśa 1.41)
Having heard this, Hiraṇyaka hastened toward Citragrīva to cut his bonds.
Thereupon Citragrīva said, "Friend, do not do this!"
"First, cut the bonds of these who have taken refuge with us;
afterwards, you shall cut my bond.
Hiraṇyaka replied, "I am of little power."
"And my teeth are tender; how then shall I be able to cut these snares? Therefore, as long as my teeth do not break—"
"In the meantime, I shall cut your bond;
immediately thereafter, I will also cut the bonds of these others as much as possible.
Citragrīva said, "Let it be so."
"Nevertheless, break their bonds to the best of your ability.
Hiraṇyaka said, "The protection of those who have sought refuge by means of sacrificing one's own self is not approved by those who know the principles of policy. For it is said:
'One should save wealth for times of calamity; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth.'"
One should always protect oneself, even at the cost of one's wife or wealth.
Furthermore:
Life is the foundation for the attainment of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
By killing it, what is not destroyed? By protecting it, what is not protected? (Hitopadeśa 1.43)
Citragrīva said: "Friend, such indeed is the way of policy;
however, I am utterly unable to endure the suffering of those who have taken refuge with me, and for that reason I speak thus. For: [The verse follows]"
A wise person should relinquish both wealth and even life for the sake of another;
when destruction is certain, it is better to give them up at the right moment. (Hitopadeśa 1.44)
This is another unique reason:
"The equality of these—birth, substance, and power—is shared by me with you.
Tell me, when and what will that fruit of my sovereignty become? (Hitopadeśa 1.45)
Moreover:
"Without even their livelihood, these [dependents] do not leave my presence;
therefore, sustain these who have taken refuge in me, even at the cost of my own life. (Hitopadeśa 1.46)
Moreover:
O friend, having abandoned all attachment to this perishable body filled with flesh, urine, excrement, and bones, protect your reputation for my sake. (Hitopadeśa 1.47)
Furthermore, consider this:
if eternal and stainless fame could be obtained through a transient body that carries impurity, would that not indeed be something gained? (Hitopadeśa 1.48)
For:
There is an immense and absolute difference between the body and its virtues;
the body perishes in an instant, while the virtues endure until the end of an aeon. (Hitopadeśa 1.49)
Having heard this, Hiraṇyaka, with a joyful mind and his hair standing on end, said: "Excellent, friend!
Excellent!
By this affection for those who have sought refuge in you, even the sovereignty over the three worlds is fitting for you."
Having spoken thus, he cut the bonds of all the pigeons.

Then Hiraṇyaka, having honored them all with great respect, said: "Friend Citragrīva, since this entanglement in the net has occurred, one should not harbor self-contempt by suspecting some fault in oneself. For: [Verse follows]"
The bird that sees its prey here from more than a hundred leagues away does not see the snare when the time for its capture has arrived. (Hitopadeśa 1.50)
Furthermore:
the eclipsing of the moon and sun by the planets,
and even the binding of elephants and serpents;
Beholding the poverty even of the wise, my thought is this: "Alas, Fate is powerful! (Hitopadeśa 1.51)
Moreover:
Even birds that roam exclusively in the sky meet with calamity;
and fish are captured by skillful men even from the unfathomable waters of the ocean.
What here is ill-conducted, and what is well-conducted? What merit is there in attaining a high position?
For Time, stretching out its hand, seizes one even from afar. (Hitopadeśa 1.52)
Having thus awakened him, offered hospitality, and embraced him, Citragrīva was sent off by him and departed with his retinue for his desired lands;
Hiraṇyaka also entered his own burrow.
Indeed, one should make hundreds of whatever friends are possible.
See how the pigeons were released from their bonds by the friend of the mouse. (Hitopadeśa 1.53)
Then a crow named Laghupatanaka, who had witnessed the entire event, said this with amazement: "O Hiranyaka!
You are praiseworthy; therefore, I too wish to form a friendship with you.
Thus, you ought to favor me with your friendship."
Having heard this, Hiraṇyaka also spoke from within his burrow: "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a crow named Laghupatanaka.
Hiraṇyaka laughed and said, "What friendship can there be between you and me? For—"
In this world, a wise person should join together that which is compatible;
for how can there be pleasure between me, who am the food, and you, who are the eater? (Hitopadeśa 1.54)
Furthermore:
"The attachment between the eater and the eaten is considered a cause of calamity; that deer, bound by a snare because of a jackal, was saved by a crow. (Hitopadeśa 1.55)
The crow asked, "How was that?
Hiraṇyaka related:
Story 2.

In the land of Magadha, there was a forest named Campakavatī. In it, a deer and a crow had lived for a long time with great affection. While that deer was wandering at will, his limbs robust and well-nourished, he was spotted by a certain jackal.
Seeing him, the jackal thought: "Ah!
How can I eat this very delicious meat?
Very well, I shall first inspire his confidence. Having reflected thus, he approached and said: "Friend, is it well with you?"
The deer asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a jackal named Kṣudrabuddhi;
bereft of kinsmen, I live here in the forest alone like one who is dead."
"Now that I have found you as a friend, I have entered the world of the living once more with a kinsman;
from this moment on, I must be your attendant in every way.
The deer replied, "So be it."
Thereafter, when the sun, the blessed garlanded with rays, had set, the two of them went to the deer's dwelling place.
There, a crow named Subuddhi, a long-time friend of the deer, lived upon a branch of a campaka tree.
Seeing them, the crow said, "Friend Citrāṅga!"
"Who is this second one?
The deer replied, "Friend,
it is not proper to form a friendship with a newcomer without cause."
Therefore, that was not a virtuous act.
And so it has been said:
"One should not give lodging to anyone whose family and character are unknown."
Indeed, through the fault of the cat, the vulture Jaradgava was killed.
The two asked, "How was that?
The crow relates:
Story 3.

On a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, there is a great *parkaṭī* tree. In its hollow, due to the adverse turn of fate, a vulture named Jaradgava dwells, his claws and eyes having fallen away.
Then, out of compassion for his livelihood, the birds living in that tree set aside small portions from their own food and give them to him.
By means of that, he lived and provided protection for those fledglings.
Then, once upon a time, a cat named Dīrghakarṇa arrived there intending to devour the fledglings.
Then, seeing him approaching, the young birds, afflicted by fear, raised a clamor. Hearing that, Jaradgava asked, "Who is this coming?
Dīrghakarṇa, looking at the vulture with fear, said, "Alas, I am lost, for he will kill me! Or rather—"
One should fear danger only as long as it has not yet arrived;
but having perceived that danger has arrived, a man should act as is appropriate. 1.57
"Now, being so very close at hand, I am unable to flee.
Therefore, let what must be happen;
for now, I shall approach him after inspiring confidence," he reflected, and having drawn near, he said to him: "Noble sir!"
"I salute you.
The vulture said, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a cat."
The vulture said: "Move far away; otherwise, you shall be killed by me.
The cat replied: "Listen first to my words;
only then, if I am worthy of death, should I be slain. For it is said:"
Is anyone ever killed or honored anywhere merely by virtue of their birth?
Having fully understood worldly convention, one becomes either subject to execution or worthy of honor.
The vulture said, "Tell me, for what purpose have you come?
He replied, "I am one who constantly bathes here on the bank of the Ganges, abstains from meat, observes celibacy, and practices the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
All the birds always praise me in your presence, saying, 'He is devoted to the knowledge of Dharma and is a ground of love and trust.'"
Therefore, I have come here to hear the Dharma from you, who are advanced in both learning and age;
and yet you, who are such knowers of the Dharma,
are prepared to kill me, a guest?
And this is the duty of a householder:
hospitality must be performed even for an enemy who has come to one's home;
a tree does not withdraw its shade even from one who has come to cut it down. (Hitopadeśa 1.59)
Furthermore, if there is no food, then even with only pleasant words, a guest must certainly be honored:
"Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech."
Even these [virtues] are never cut off in the house of the righteous.
Furthermore:
Whether he be a child, an old man, or a youth, if he has come to one's house, honor must be rendered to him; for every guest is venerable.
Furthermore:
"The virtuous show compassion even toward beings devoid of merit;
for the moon does not withhold its moonlight from the house of a *caṇḍāla*. (Hitopadeśa 1.62)
And furthermore:
"When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, he departs having bestowed his own misdeeds upon that person and taking away their merit. (Hitopadeśa 1.63)
And furthermore:
Even one of low birth who has come to the house of the highest caste is to be honored as is appropriate, for the guest embodies all the gods. (Hitopadeśa 1.64)
The vulture said, "A cat indeed has a taste for meat,
and young birds dwell here;
therefore, I alone speak thus."
Having heard this, the cat touched the ground and his ears, and said: "Having studied the Dharma-śāstras, I have undertaken with dispassion this difficult vow of Cāndrāyaṇa.
For even among the Dharma-śāstras that dispute one another, there is a consensus on this point: non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the highest dharma. As it is said:"
Those men who have desisted from all violence, who endure everything,
and who have become a refuge for all— those men go to heaven.
And furthermore:
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else goes to destruction along with the body. (Hitopadeśa 1.66)
Furthermore:
"When one eats the flesh of another at a certain time, observe the difference between the two:
for one there is a momentary pleasure, while the other is deprived of life. (Hitopadeśa 1.67)
Moreover:
"By means of the suffering that arises in a person at the thought 'I must die,' it is possible through inference to protect others as well. (Hitopadeśa 1.68)
Listen further:
even with wild vegetables growing spontaneously in the forest, this wretched belly is filled;
for its sake, who would commit a great sin? (Hitopadeśa 1.69)
Having thus inspired confidence, that cat remained in the hollow of a tree.
Then, as the days passed, he would seize the young birds, bring them to his own hollow, and eat them every day.
Now, those whose offspring had been devoured—
Afflicted by grief and lamenting here and there, they began an investigation.
Having learned of this, the cat emerged from the hollow and fled outside.
Afterwards, as the birds searched here and there, they all concluded that the young ones had been eaten in that tree-hollow, and the vulture was killed.
Therefore I say: "To one whose family and character are unknown," and so forth.
Having heard this, the jackal said with anger: "On the very day you first saw the deer, you too were one whose family and character were unknown.
So how is it that your affection for him increases more and more? Or rather—
Where there are no wise men, even one of little intellect is praiseworthy;
in a land devoid of trees, even the castor-oil plant passes for a tree.
Furthermore:
"The calculation of 'this one is my own' or 'that one is a stranger' belongs to those of small minds; for those of noble conduct, however, the entire earth is but a single family. (Hitopadeśa 1.71)

"Just as this deer is my kinsman, so too are you. The deer asked, "What is the use of this back-and-forth? Let us all remain together, experiencing happiness through confidential conversation. For it is said:
No one is anyone's friend, nor is anyone anyone's enemy;
through worldly dealings, friends and likewise enemies are born.
The crow said, "So be it.
Then, in the morning, they all went to their respective desired places.
Once, the jackal spoke secretly to the deer: "Friend, deer!"
"In this very part of the forest, there is a field full of grain;
I will take you there and show it to you.
When this was done, the deer went there every day and ate the grain.
Then, after a few days, the owner of the field saw that and set snares there.

Soon after, the deer returned; while grazing there, he was caught by the snares and thought: "Who other than a friend is capable of saving me from this hunter’s snare, which is like the noose of Death?
In the meantime, a jackal arrived at the spot and thought: "Our scheme has indeed borne fruit."
The fulfillment of my desire will also come about through abundance;
for as this [being] is being cooked, its bones smeared with flesh and blood must necessarily be obtained by me,
and they shall become my food in great measure.
And that deer, seeing him, was filled with joy and said: "Friend, cut my bonds first;
save me quickly! For it is said:"
One should recognize a friend in times of adversity, a hero in battle, an honest man in matters of debt, a wife when wealth has been exhausted, and kinsmen in times of calamity. (Hitopadeśa 1.73)
Furthermore:
"He who stands by one during a festival, in times of calamity, during famine, in the peril of enemies, at the royal court, and in the cremation ground—he is a kinsman. (Hitopadeśa 1.74)
The jackal, looking repeatedly at the snare, thought: "This bond is indeed firm.
And he said: "Friend, these snares are made of sinews."
"Therefore, today, on the day of the Lord, how can I touch these with my teeth? Friend,
if you do not think otherwise in your heart,
then in the morning you must do what you have said."
Immediately thereafter, that crow, seeing that the deer had not returned at nightfall, searched here and there; upon finding him in such a state, he said, "Friend, what is this?
The deer replied, "This is the fruit of disregarding the words of a friend. And so it is said:
He who does not listen to the speech of friends who desire his welfare..."
Calamity is close at hand for him; that man is a source of joy to his enemies.
The crow said, "Where is that deceiver? Where does he stay?
The deer replied, "Desiring my flesh, he remains right here.
The crow said, "Friend!"
I have already said before:
"I have no fault"—this is not a ground for trust;
for even those possessed of virtues have cause for fear from the cruel. (Hitopadeśa 1.76)
Those whose life-span has come to an end do not smell the fragrance of a lamp being extinguished, do not hear the words of a friend, and do not see the star Arundhatī. (Hitopadeśa 1.77)
One should avoid such a friend who ruins one's affairs in one's absence but speaks pleasantly in one's presence; he is like a jar of poison with milk on its surface. (Hitopadeśa 1.78)
Then the crow, sighing deeply, said: "O deceiver!
What evil deed has been committed by you? For—those who have been addressed with sweet words..."
For those who have been brought under control by false pretenses,
who possess hope and faith in the world—
what is there for those seekers that they ought to be deceived? (Hitopadeśa 1.79)
Moreover:
O Blessed Earth, how can you bear that person who is false to his word and commits evil against one who has been helpful, trusting, and pure-minded? (Hitopadeśa 1.80)
One should not cultivate friendship or enmity with a wicked person;
for hot charcoal burns the hand, while cold charcoal blackens it. (Hitopadeśa 1.81)
Or rather, this is the way of wicked people: first they fall at one's feet, then they devour the flesh of one's back,
and finally they whisper some strange fruit of advice softly into one's ear.
Having detected a vulnerability, the mosquito enters suddenly and without hesitation; indeed, it performs every kind of mischief characteristic of a wicked person.
And so it is said:
"A wicked person who speaks kindly—this is no cause for trust;
honey rests upon the tip of his tongue, but in his heart lies the *hālāhala* poison. (Hitopadeśa 1.83)
Then at dawn, as the field-owner approached that place with a club in his hand, he was spotted by the crow.
Having observed him, the crow said: "Friend deer, remain there showing yourself as if dead, filling your belly with air and keeping your legs stiff."
"I shall scratch at your eyes with my beak;
when I make a sound, you must rise up and flee quickly."
The deer remained exactly as he was at the word of the crow.
Then, with eyes wide open in joy, the owner of the field beheld the deer in such a state. Thereupon, he exclaimed: "Ah!"
"Are you dead yourself?
Having said this, he released the deer from its bonds and hurried to gather up the snares.
Then, when the field-owner had moved some distance away, the deer, hearing the sound of the crow, quickly rose and fled.
Aiming at him, the owner of that field, provoked to anger, struck the jackal with a club and killed him.
And so it has been said:
"In three years, in three months, in three fortnights, or in three days..."
One experiences the fruit of extremely intense sins and merits right here in this very life.
Therefore I say: "The affection between the eater and the food," and so forth.
Thus ends the story of the deer, the crow, and the jackal.
Then the crow spoke again:
"O sinless one, even though you have been eaten, my food is not yet sufficient;
for as long as you live, I shall live, just like Citragrīva."
Moreover:
Trust is seen even among animals who perform only meritorious deeds;
for the innate nature of the virtuous does not change because of their excellent character. (1.86)
Furthermore: Even when provoked to anger, the mind of a virtuous person does not undergo transformation;
for it is impossible to heat the waters of the ocean with a torch of straw. (Hitopadeśa 1.87)
Hiraṇyaka said: "You are fickle;
one should never form a friendship with a fickle person.
As it has been said:"
The cat, the buffalo, the ram, the crow, and likewise the base man—these prevail through trust; therefore, trust is not beneficial in such cases.
Furthermore: you belong to the faction of our enemy;
one should not form an alliance with an enemy.
And this has been said:
One should not form an alliance with an enemy, even through a closely knit treaty;
for water, even when thoroughly heated, still extinguishes fire.
A wicked person should be avoided even if he is adorned with learning; is a snake not terrifying, even when decorated with a jewel? (Hitopadeśa 1.90)
That which is impossible cannot be made possible; that which is possible is indeed possible.
A cart does not travel on water, nor does a boat go upon dry land. (Hitopadeśa 1.91)
Furthermore:
He who places his trust in enemies, even for the sake of a great and essential purpose, or in wives who are estranged, his life ends with that. (Hitopadeśa 1.92)
Laghupatanaka said: "I have heard everything;
nevertheless, my resolve is this alone:
that you must certainly cultivate friendship with me."
"Otherwise, I shall destroy myself by fasting at your door. For thus it is:
a wicked person is as easy to break as a clay pot, yet difficult to mend; a good person, however, is as hard to break as a golden vessel, yet is easily mended. (Hitopadeśa 1.93)
Moreover:
"From the fluidity of all metals, from the instincts of beasts and birds, from fear and greed in fools, and from the sight of the company of the virtuous. (Hitopadeśa 1.94)
Furthermore:
"For friends are seen to be like coconuts—beautiful only on the outside; others are like jujubes—charming only from the exterior. (Hitopadeśa 1.95)
Furthermore:
Even when their bonds of affection are severed, the virtues of the holy do not undergo change;
for even when lotus stalks are broken, their fibers remain connected. (Hitopadeśa 1.96)
Furthermore:
Purity, generosity, valor, equanimity toward pleasure and pain, courtesy, devotion, and truthfulness are the qualities of a friend. (Hitopadeśa 1.97)
"Endowed with such virtues as these, what friend other than you could I have found?
Having heard these and other words of his, Hiraṇyaka went outside and said: "I have been refreshed by this nectar of your speech.
And so it is said:"
Neither a bath in very cool water, nor a string of pearls,
nor an application of sandalwood paste— even when applied to every limb— brings such comfort to one afflicted by heat as the speech of a virtuous person generally brings to the heart for its delight.
And when refined by sound reasoning, it is like a magnetizing mantra for those who have performed virtuous deeds. (1.98)
Furthermore:
"The betrayal of secrets, begging, cruelty due to a fickle mind, anger, untruthfulness, and gambling—these are what ruin a friend. (Hitopadeśa 1.99)
By this sequence of speech, not even a single fault is perceived in you; for:
"Proficiency and truthfulness are understood through the course of conversation;
lack of arrogance and steadiness are apprehended through direct observation. (Hitopadeśa 1.100)
Furthermore:
For the friendship of one whose inner self is pure is of one kind, while the speech of one whose mind is afflicted by deceit proceeds in quite another way. (Hitopadeśa 1.101)
The wicked have one thing in their minds, another in their speech, and another in their actions;
the great-souled have one thing in their minds, one in their speech, and one in their actions.

"So be it; let it be exactly as you desire," said Hiraṇyaka, and having established a friendship and gratified the crow with various kinds of food, he entered his burrow. The crow also went to his own place. From that time forward, some time passed for the two of them through the giving of food to one another, inquiries after each other's welfare, and confidential conversations.
One day, Laghupatanaka said to Hiraṇyaka: "Friend!"
"This place provides food for a crow that is most difficult to obtain;
therefore, I wish to abandon it and go to another location.
Hiranyaka said:
"Teeth, hair, nails, and men do not look well when displaced from their proper positions.
Having understood this, a wise person should not abandon his own place. (Hitopadeśa 1.103)
The crow said: "Friend, this is the speech of a base man. For it is said:
'Lions, noble men, and elephants depart, leaving their place behind.'"
In that very place, crows, base men, and deer meet their end.
Furthermore:
What is considered one's own domain or what is a foreign land for a wise hero?
Whatever country he takes refuge in, that very place he makes his own through the prowess of his arms.
When a lion, whose weapons are his fangs, claws, and tail, enters the forest, it quenches its own thirst with the very blood of the lordly elephants slain therein. (Hitopadeśa 1.105)
Hiraṇyaka said: "Friend, where should we go?
For it is said:
'The wise man moves with one foot while standing firm with the other.'"
One should not abandon one's former dwelling without having first examined another place.
The crow said, "Friend,
there is a well-surveyed place.
Hiraṇyaka asked, "What is it?"
The crow said: "In the Daṇḍaka forest there is a lake named Karpūragaura.
There dwells a tortoise named Manthara, a long-time friend of mine who is naturally virtuous.
Look, my friend!"
Skill in instructing others is easy for all men to achieve; but the personal practice of dharma belongs only to some great soul. (Hitopadeśa 1.107)
"And he will nourish me with excellent foods.
Hiraṇyaka also said: "In that case, what should I do by remaining here? For:
In whatever land there is no honor, no livelihood, and no kinsmen..."
And no one who has acquired knowledge should ever avoid that place.
Furthermore:
A creditor, a learned brahmin, a king, a river, and fifthly, a physician—one should not make one's dwelling where these five are not found. (Hitopadeśa 1.109)
Furthermore:
"The course of worldly life, fear, shame, courtesy, and a disposition toward generosity—if these five are not found in a place, one should not make one's dwelling there. (Hitopadeśa 1.110)
And furthermore,
O friend: one should not dwell in a place where these four things are not present.
A creditor, a physician, a learned Vedic scholar, and a river with water. (1.111)
"Therefore, lead me there as well.
The crow said, "So be it.
Then the crow, accompanied by that friend, went to the vicinity of the lake, enjoying the pleasure of various conversations.
Then Manthara, seeing Laghupatanaka from afar, rose up and, having performed the appropriate hospitality, offered guest-reception even to the mouse. For it is said:
Whether he be a child, an old man, or a youth, whoever comes to one’s house, him one must honor; everywhere a guest is venerable. (Hitopadeśa 1.112)
Likewise:
"For the twice-born, the fire is the preceptor; for the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor;
for women, the husband alone is the preceptor; and everywhere, the guest is the preceptor. (Hitopadeśa 1.113)
Furthermore:
Even if he is of low birth, a guest who has come to the house of one of the highest caste is to be honored as is appropriate, for the guest embodies all the gods. (Hitopadeśa 1.114)
The crow said: "Friend Manthara,
perform for me a particularly distinguished honor."

"Since this king of mice named Hiraṇyaka is the foremost among those of meritorious deeds and a treasure-mine of compassion—if even the King of Serpents were somehow capable of praising his virtues with two thousand tongues," having said this, he related the story of Citragrīva.
Then Manthara, having respectfully honored Hiraṇyaka, said: "O noble one!"
"You ought to tell me the reason for your coming to this desolate forest.
Hiraṇyaka said, "I shall tell you; listen.
Story 4.
In a city named Campakā, there was a monastery for wandering mendicants. There lived a wandering mendicant named Cūḍākarṇa.
He would place his alms bowl, containing the remnants of the food he had received as alms, upon a peg and go to sleep.
And I, leaping up again and again, ate that food every day.

Shortly thereafter, a wandering mendicant named Vīṇākarṇa, a dear friend of his, arrived; while he was engaged in various conversations with him, Cūḍākarṇa struck the ground with a piece of a worn-out bamboo pole in order to frighten me.
Seeing him in such a state, Vīṇākarṇa said: "Friend, why have you become indifferent to my story and attached to something else? For your face is serene and your gaze is clear."
A passion for conversation, sweet speech,
excessive affection, and an appearance of agitation— these are the marks of a person who is constantly devoted.
Not looking at him, destroying what was done before,
speaking of his misdeeds,
and forgetting his name during the course of conversation.
This is the characteristic of a person whose mind is free from passion.
Cūḍākarṇa said: "My good man, I am not disenchanted;
however, look, this mouse is my enemy, for it constantly leaps up and eats the alms-food placed in my bowl."
Vīṇākarṇa, having observed the ivory peg, said: "How is it that this mouse, though possessing such little strength, leaps so far?
There must be some reason for this.
After reflecting for a moment, the wandering mendicant said: "In this matter, it appears that the cause is indeed an abundance of wealth. For:"
In this world, everyone is always and everywhere possessed of wealth and power;
for even the sovereignty of kings arises from the root of wealth.

Then, having taken a spade and dug a hole with that mendicant, my long-accumulated wealth was seized. From that time forth, being deprived of my own strength and lacking the energy of a living being, I became unable even to procure my own food; as I was crawling very slowly, Cūḍākarṇa saw me and said:
The world is powerful through wealth; through wealth one becomes wise.
Behold this wicked mouse, who has returned to the common state of his own kind. (Hitopadeśa 1.118)
Furthermore:
"But for a man of small intelligence who is deprived of wealth, all his undertakings perish like small streams in the summer heat. (Hitopadeśa 1.119)
Furthermore:
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world; indeed, he who has wealth is a wise man.
Furthermore:
"The house of one without a son is empty; so is that of one devoid of true friends.
For a fool, all directions are empty; but poverty is the emptiness of everything. (Hitopadeśa 1.121)
Furthermore:
Between poverty and death, poverty is considered the lesser of the two;
for death involves little suffering, whereas poverty is exceedingly difficult to endure. (Hitopadeśa 1.122)
And furthermore:
those very senses are unimpaired, that same intellect is indeed unimpeded, and the speech is that very same.
It is truly strange that a man, when deprived of the warmth of wealth, becomes someone else in an instant. (Hitopadeśa 1.123)
Having heard all this, I reflected: "My remaining here for food is no longer appropriate now.
And so it has been said:
"When fate is utterly adverse and human effort is rendered futile..."
For a high-minded man who is poor, where else but in the forest can there be happiness?
And furthermore:
A man of spirit may indeed die, but he never succumbs to wretchedness;
even fire reaches extinction, but it never becomes cold. (Hitopadeśa 1.125)
Furthermore:
"Like a cluster of flowers, there are only two courses for a wise man:
he should either stand at the head of all, or else wither away in the forest. (Hitopadeśa 1.126)
Furthermore, it is improper to recount this account to another; for:
"A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, domestic misconduct, deception, or humiliation. (Hitopadeśa 1.127)

Moreover, living here by means of begging is also exceedingly contemptible; for it is said: "It is better that fire be satiated with life-breaths by one devoid of wealth than that a wretched person, fallen from proper conduct, be entreated. (Hitopadeśa 1.128)
Furthermore:

Through poverty one comes to lose self-respect; being overcome by shame, one falls away from courage; lacking courage, one is treated with contempt; and through such contempt, one falls into despondency.
One who is despondent falls into grief; one overwhelmed by grief is abandoned by wisdom;
and one devoid of wisdom goes to ruin. Alas! Death is the abode of all calamities.
Moreover:
It is better for one to observe silence than to speak a falsehood;
it is better for men to be impotent than to approach another's wife.
It is better to give up one's life than to take pleasure in the words of the malicious; it is better to subsist on alms than to find joy in tasting the wealth of others.
An empty hall is better than a wicked bull; a courtesan as a wife is better than an undisciplined woman of good family;
dwelling in the forest is better than living in a city ruled by one who lacks discernment.
It is better to give up one's life than to associate with the base. (Hitopadeśa 1.131)
Moreover—

just as service destroys all pride, moonlight dispels darkness, old age robs beauty, and the story of Hari and Hara removes sin, so too does the pursuit of wealth destroy even a hundred virtues. (Hitopadeśa 1.132)
"So why do I nourish myself with the food of others?
Alas, what misery!
That too is a second door to death. And furthermore—"
The sick man is a long-term traveler, eating the food of others and sleeping in the dwellings of others;
what he calls life is death, and what he calls death is his rest.
Having reflected thus, yet out of greed I again made an effort to take his food.
And so it has been said:
"Through greed the intellect wavers; greed gives rise to thirst."
Afflicted by thirst, a person experiences suffering both in this world and in the next.
Then, approaching very slowly, I was struck by that Vīṇākarṇa with a piece of a worn-out bamboo pole, and I thought: "For one who is greedy and discontented is inevitably a self-betrayer.
And so it is said:
'One who is greedy for wealth, being discontented, lacks self-restraint and has no control over his senses.'"
For one whose mind is contented, there are indeed no misfortunes whatsoever.
All prosperity belongs to him whose mind is content;
for one whose feet are covered by shoes, is not the entire earth as if covered with leather? (Hitopadeśa 1.136)
Furthermore:
"The happiness of those with peaceful minds, who are satisfied by the nectar of contentment—whence could that come for those greedy for wealth, who run hither and thither? (Hitopadeśa 1.137)
Moreover:
"By him has everything been studied and heard, by him has everything been practiced, who, having cast all hopes behind him, has taken hold of hopelessness. (Hitopadeśa 1.138)
Moreover:
Blessed is the life of someone who has not served at the gate of a lord, who has never witnessed the pain of separation, and who has never uttered the words of a coward. (Hitopadeśa 1.139)
For one driven by craving, even a hundred yojanas is not too far;
for one who is content, there is no regard even for wealth already in the palm of his hand. (Hitopadeśa 1.140)
Therefore, in this matter, discerning the action appropriate to one's situation is best.

What is dharma? Compassion for living beings. What is happiness? Constant freedom from illness in this world. What is affection? A virtuous disposition. What is wisdom? Discernment. (Hitopadeśa 1.141)
And so it is said:
"For discernment is true wisdom; when calamities have befallen, they are for those who possess discernment, but for those who lack it, disasters shall occur at every step. (Hitopadeśa 1.142)
For it is said:
One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of a family; one should sacrifice a family for the sake of a village;
one should sacrifice a village for the sake of a country; and one should sacrifice the whole earth for the sake of the self. (Hitopadeśa 1.143)
Furthermore:
Whether it be water obtained without effort or delicious food accompanied by great fear, I consider that indeed to be happiness wherein there is peace. (Hitopadeśa 1.144)
Having reflected thus, I have come to this uninhabited forest; for—
better is the forest frequented by tigers and lordly elephants, where one dwells in the shelter of trees and subsists on leaves, fruits, and water.
Grass for a bed and bark for clothing—
living among one's kinsmen while destitute of wealth is not such a life.
Therefore:
"In this tree of the objects of worldly existence, there are only two fruits that possess flavor:
the tasting of the nectar of poetry and association with virtuous people. (Hitopadeśa 1.146)
Furthermore:

Association with the virtuous, devotion to Keśava, and immersion in the waters of the Gaṅgā—these three, indeed, one should cultivate as the essences within this worthless cycle of existence. (Hitopadeśa 1.147)
Manthara said:
Wealth is like the dust on one's feet; youth is like the rush of a mountain river; life is as fickle and fleeting as a drop of water; and existence is like foam.
He who, with a steady mind, does not practice the Dharma that unlocks the bolt of heaven, is later tormented by remorse; when he has grown old, he is consumed by the fire of grief.
"You have made excessive accumulations;
this is the fault of that. Listen:
for wealth that has been acquired, renunciation alone is its true preservation."
Just as water residing within the belly of a pond flows out through an overflow channel.
And furthermore:
Whatever wealth the miser buried deeper and deeper in the earth, he thereby first prepared a path for himself to go to his abode below. (Hitopadeśa 1.150)
For it is said:
He who desires the acquisition of wealth while obstructing his own happiness is merely a vessel for suffering, like one who carries the burden of another's interests. (Hitopadeśa 1.151)
And so it has been said:
"If we were wealthy by means of wealth that is devoid of both giving and enjoyment, then why are we not wealthy by that very same wealth? (Hitopadeśa 1.152)
For it is said:
What is the use of wealth for one who neither gives nor enjoys it?
And what is the use of strength for one who does not subdue his enemies?
What is the use of sacred learning for one who does not practice righteousness?
What is the use of a self for one who has not conquered his senses? (Hitopadeśa 1.153)
Furthermore:
The wealth of a miser is common to others because he does not enjoy it;
the connection that "this belongs to him" is only realized through the suffering that arises when it is lost. (Hitopadeśa 1.154)
Moreover:
Neither to a god, nor to a Brahmin, nor to kinsmen, nor even to oneself does the wealth of a miser go; it is taken away by fire, thieves, and kings.
And so it has been said:
"Generosity accompanied by kind speech, knowledge free from pride, and valor endowed with patience."
Generosity and wealth combined— this fourfold excellence is difficult to find.
And it is said:
One should always practice accumulation, but one should not engage in excessive accumulation;
for this jackal, being habituated to excessive accumulation, was killed by a bow. (Hitopadeśa 1.157)
The two of them asked, "How was that?
Manthara relates the story—
Story 5.
There was a hunter named Bhairava, a resident of Kalyāṇakaṭaka.
Once, greedy for meat, he took up his bow and went into the middle of the Vindhya forest in search of game;
there, he killed a deer.
Then, as he was going along carrying the deer, he saw a boar of fearsome appearance.
Thereupon, having set the deer on the ground, he struck the boar with an arrow.
The boar also came forward and, letting out a roar as terrible as the clouds at the end of an aeon, struck the hunter in the groin; he fell down like a tree cut at its roots.
And so it has been said:
"Water, fire, poison, a weapon, hunger, disease, or falling from a mountain—having encountered some such cause, the embodied being is released from life. (Hitopadeśa 1.158)
Then, by the trampling of their feet, one snake also died.
In the meantime, a jackal named Dīrgharāva, wandering about in search of food, saw those dead deer, hunter, snake, and boar. Having seen them, he thought: "Oh, what good fortune!"
"Today a great feast has come to me;
or rather,
just as unforeseen sufferings come upon embodied beings."
I consider pleasures to be likewise; in this matter, destiny prevails.
A man travels for one month; deer and boars for two months;
a snake travels for a single day; today, the bowstring is to be eaten. (Hitopadeśa 1.160)
Then, at the first onset of hunger, he said, "I shall eat this tasteless sinew-string attached to the bow," and did so.
When the sinew-string was severed, the bow sprang up suddenly and pierced Dīrgharāva in the heart; thus, he met his death.
Therefore, I say: "One should always make an accumulation," and so forth. And likewise:
"Whatever one gives away and whatever one eats—that alone is the wealth of the wealthy;
others play with the wife and the riches of the deceased. (Hitopadeśa 1.161)
Furthermore:
"Whatever you give to distinguished persons and whatever you eat day by day—that, I consider, is your wealth; the rest you merely guard for someone else. (Hitopadeśa 1.162)
Let it be; what is the use now of describing what has already passed? For:
Men of wise intellect do not long for what is unattainable, they do not wish to grieve over what is lost, and they do not lose their composure even in times of calamity. (Hitopadeśa 1.163)
Therefore, my friend, you must always remain full of enthusiasm;
for— Even after studying the scriptures, people remain fools; but that man who puts them into practice is truly wise.
Even a well-prepared medicine does not cure the ailments of the sick merely by its name. (Hitopadeśa 1.164)
And furthermore: indeed,
the method of higher knowledge does not produce even the slightest merit for one who is timid regarding resolute application.
For one who is blind, does a lamp illuminate an object even when it is held in the palm of his hand? (Hitopadeśa 1.165)
Therefore, my friend, you must bring peace here with the remaining ten years;
you should not consider even this to be excessively painful.
One should experience happiness when it comes, and likewise, one should experience suffering when it comes.
Sufferings and pleasures revolve like a wheel.
Furthermore:
Just as frogs come to a watering hole, or birds to a lake filled with water, all forms of prosperity approach a man who is industrious, even against his will. (Hitopadeśa 1.167)
Moreover:

Fortune herself desires to dwell with one who is endowed with energy, who does not procrastinate, who knows the proper method of action, who is unattached to vices, who is brave, grateful, and firm in friendship. (Hitopadeśa 1.168)
And specifically:
even without wealth, the steadfast man attains a state of high esteem; whereas the miser, though possessed of wealth, falls into a state of contempt.
Can even a dog, though wearing a golden necklace, ever attain the lion-like splendor that arises from its own nature and consists in the acquisition of a multitude of virtues?
Furthermore:
"Why indeed do you take pride in being wealthy? Why do you fall into despair when your fortune has departed?
For the rises and falls of human beings are like a ball struck by the hand. (Hitopadeśa 1.170)
Furthermore:
One does not strive excessively for the sake of livelihood, for that has been ordained by the Creator itself;
as soon as a creature emerges from the womb, the mother's breasts begin to flow.
Moreover, friend, listen: he by whom the swans were made white, the parrots were made green,
and the peacocks were adorned with their patterns— he shall provide for your livelihood.

Furthermore, O friend, hear this secret of the virtuous: "Wealth produces suffering in its acquisition, causes torment in times of misfortune, and deludes one in prosperity; how, then, can wealth bring happiness? (Hitopadeśa 1.173)
Furthermore:
For one who desires half of the Dharma, it is better to have no desire at all;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. (Hitopadeśa 1.174)
For it is said:
"Just as meat is devoured by birds in the sky, by beasts of prey on the earth, and by fish in the water, so too is the man of wealth preyed upon everywhere. (Hitopadeśa 1.175)
Moreover:

For those possessed of wealth, there is constant fear from kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, and even from their own kinsmen, just as for living beings there is constant fear of death. (Hitopadeśa 1.176)
For instance:
In this birth so full of afflictions, what indeed could be more painful than this—that there is no fulfillment of one's desires, and yet desire does not cease? (Hitopadeśa 1.177)
Moreover, brother, listen:
wealth is difficult to acquire; even when acquired, it is preserved with great effort.
The loss of what has been acquired is like death; therefore, one should not worry about this. (Hitopadeśa 1.178)
If that craving is abandoned, who is poor and who is wealthy? But if its course is permitted, servitude rests upon one's head.
Furthermore:
Whatever one may desire, from that very thing desire proceeds;
for when that object is actually attained, it is in fact the cessation of desire that occurs. (Hitopadeśa 1.180)
What need is there for much? Let us spend our time here in confidential conversation with one another; for— "Affections and angers end with death, and even abandonments are momentary and fleeting;
yet among the great-souled, there is no such thing as a total renunciation. (Hitopadeśa 1.181)
Having heard this, Laghupatanaka said: "Blessed are you, Manthara!
You are to be sought as a refuge in every way; for—only the virtuous are always capable of rescuing the virtuous from calamity."
For elephants mired in the mud, only elephants are capable of bearing the burden.
Furthermore:
He alone among men on earth is praiseworthy;
he is the most excellent, the virtuous man, and he is blessed.
For those who come as supplicants or have sought refuge,
they do not depart with their hopes shattered or turned away.
Thus, living as they pleased in food and recreation, they dwelt there contentedly and happily.
Then, on one occasion, a deer named Citrāṅga, having been frightened by someone, arrived and joined them.
Suspecting that the cause of fear was approaching behind him, Manthara entered the water.
The mouse entered its burrow,
and the crow also flew up and perched on the top of a tree.
Then, after Laghupatanaka had searched far and wide, he found no cause for fear whatsoever.
Afterwards, having returned at his word, they all gathered together and sat down right there.
Manthara said, "My dear deer, is it well with you? May you enjoy food, water, and so forth according to your own desire."
"By staying here, let this forest be provided with a protector.
Citrāṅga said, "Terrified by the hunter, I have come to you for refuge;
therefore, I desire friendship with you all."

And may you favor me with compassion and loving-kindness; for it is said by the wise: "Whether out of greed or even out of fear, he who abandons one who has come for refuge incurs a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (Hitopadeśa 1.184)
Hiraṇyaka also said: "Friendship with us has already been established for you without effort;
for— [It arises] from being born of one's own body, from a formal alliance, or likewise through hereditary succession."
A friend who protects one from calamities—thus should a friend be known to be of four kinds.
"Therefore, please stay here as if in your own home.
Hearing this, the deer became joyful; having taken his food at will and drunk water, he sat down in the shade of a banyan tree near the water.
Then Manthara said, "Friend deer!"
"By whom have you been frightened?
Do hunters ever roam in this desolate forest?
The deer replied, "In the kingdom of Kaliṅga, there is a king named Rukmāṅgada."

"And he, having arrived in the course of his expedition of world conquest, is currently encamped on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā; furthermore, a rumor is heard from the mouths of hunters that he will come here tomorrow morning and be near the Karpūra lake.
Therefore, considering that staying here tomorrow morning would be a cause for danger, let what must be done be undertaken accordingly."
Having heard that, the tortoise said with fear, "Friend,
let us go to another body of water.
The crow and the deer also said, "Friend, so be it."
Hiraṇyaka reflected and said: "When Manthara has reached the water again, he will be safe; but what provision is there for him as he travels on land?
Water is the fortress of aquatic creatures, and a fortress is the refuge of those who dwell within it."
For beasts of prey and the like, their own territory is their strength; for kings, the army is their supreme power.
For that which can be accomplished by means cannot be accomplished by sheer valor;
a female crow caused a black snake to be killed by means of a golden thread.
For example—
Story 6:
In Brahmāraṇya there was an elephant named Karpūratilaka.
Seeing him, all the jackals thought:
"If he can be killed by some means or other, then for four months we would have food at our own pleasure from his body."
Then, from among them, one old jackal made a vow:
"By the power of my intellect, I must bring about his death.
Immediately thereafter, that deceiver went to Karpūratilaka, prostrated himself with the eight-limbed salutation, and said: "O King!"
"Grant me the favor of your sight.
The elephant asked, "Who are you?
From where have you come?"

He said: "I am a jackal, sent to your presence by all the forest-dwelling animals who have assembled together, for it is not proper to remain without a king. Therefore, you—who are endowed with the qualities of a sovereign lord—have been chosen to be consecrated here in this forest kingdom. For it is said:"
One who is exceedingly pure through family and popular customs, powerful, righteous, and skilled in statesmanship—such a master is fit for the earth. (Hitopadeśa 1.188)
Furthermore, observe this:
one should first seek a king, then a wife, and then wealth.
If there is no king in this world, where is the wife? Where is the wealth? (Hitopadeśa 1.189)
And furthermore:
Like the rain-cloud, the lord of the earth is the support of all beings; for even when the rain-cloud fails, one may still live, but not when the king fails.
Furthermore:
In this world, which is generally subject to others, one who abides within fixed boundaries is rare due to the application of punishment; thus, virtuous conduct is difficult to find.
Even if her husband is emaciated, crippled, diseased, or impoverished, a woman of noble family attends to him out of fear of punishment.
"Acting so that the auspicious hour does not pass, may Your Majesty come quickly.
Having said this, he rose and departed.
Then Karpūratilaka, drawn by the prospect of obtaining the kingdom, ran along the path shown by the jackal and sank into a great mire.
The elephant said: "Friend jackal, what should be done now?
I have fallen into a great mire and am dying."
Turning around, look!
The jackal said with a laugh, "O King,
place your hand on the tip of my tail and stand up!"
Since you have placed your trust in the words of one such as I,
this is the fruit thereof:
experience now this refuge-less suffering.
And so it has been said:
"When you are free from the company of the good, you will fall;
when you fall into the assemblies of the wicked, you will perish. (Hitopadeśa 1.192)
Then the elephant, submerged in the great mire, was devoured by the jackals.
Therefore I say: "For that which can be accomplished by means," and so forth.
Then, disregarding those words for his welfare, Manthara, as if bewildered by great fear, abandoned that body of water and set out.
Hiraṇyaka and the others also followed him out of affection, fearing some misfortune.
Then, as he was traveling on land, Manthara was encountered by a certain hunter wandering in the forest.
Having seized him and lifted him up, the hunter fastened him to his bow, saying, "I am fortunate! and, distressed by hunger and thirst from the fatigue of his wandering, set off toward his own home.
Then those deer, crow, and mouse fell into great despair and followed after him.
Thereupon Hiraṇyaka lamented:
"Before I can reach the end of even a single sorrow, it is as if I have not reached the further shore of the ocean."
Just then, a second [danger] has presented itself to me; through such vulnerabilities, misfortunes multiply.
But that friend who is born of one's own nature arises solely through good fortune; possessing unfeigned affection, he does not abandon one even in times of adversity. (Hitopadeśa 1.194)
Moreover:
"Men do not place such trust in a mother, nor in a wife, nor in a uterine brother, nor even in a son, as they do in a friend born of their own nature. (Hitopadeśa 1.195)
Having reflected thus repeatedly, he said: "Alas, what misfortune is mine!
For— The sequences of one's own karmic actions, consisting of auspicious and inauspicious deeds, manifest at different points in time."
Right here, I have seen these very states of affairs as if they were my own past lives.
Or rather, it is exactly thus:
the body is accompanied by imminent ruin; prosperity is the seat of calamities;
meetings end in partings; everything that arises is fragile.
Reflecting further, he said:
"By whom was this jewel created—the two syllables 'mitra' (friend)—which is a protection from sorrow, enmity, and fear, and a vessel for joy and confidence? (Hitopadeśa 1.198)
Furthermore:
A friend is an elixir of affection for the eyes and a delight for the mind; such a person, who is an equal vessel for both joy and sorrow, is found only by those of meritorious soul.
Other friends who, driven by a desire for wealth, gather around one at the time of prosperity—they all meet everywhere; but adversity is the touchstone for their true nature.
Having lamented thus at length, Hiraṇyaka said to Citrāṅga and Laghupatanaka: "While this hunter has not yet departed from the forest, let an effort be made to liberate Manthara.
They both replied: "Instruct us quickly as to what must be done."
Hiraṇyaka said, "Citrāṅga should go near the water and show himself as if dead and motionless;
the crow, perching upon him, should scratch at him with its beak.
Surely that hunter, seeking deer meat, will abandon the tortoise there and go his way."
"Therefore, I shall cut the bonds of Manthara.
When the hunter is nearby, you two must flee.
Then Citrāṅga and Laghupatanaka went quickly and acted accordingly; the exhausted hunter, having drunk water, sat down beneath a tree and saw him in such a state.
He saw a deer;
then, having placed the tortoise near the water and taken up a knife, he set out toward the deer with a joyful heart.
In the meantime, Hiraṇyaka arrived and cut Manthara’s bonds.

With its bonds severed, the tortoise quickly entered the lake; and that deer, seeing the hunter close by, rose up and fled swiftly. When the hunter returned and reached the foot of the tree, not seeing the tortoise, he thought: "This is indeed fitting for me, who acted without due reflection. For it is said:"
He who abandons certainties and pursues uncertainties loses his certainties;
for that which is uncertain is already lost.
Then, due to the power of his own karma, he entered the camp despondent;
and Manthara and all the others, having escaped calamity, went to their own places and remained there at ease. Then the princes said joyfully: "We have all heard it; we are happy."
"Our desire has been fulfilled.
Viṣṇuśarman said: "This which you desired has indeed been accomplished; may this further wish also be granted:"
May virtuous people find friends throughout the lands; may prosperity be attained;
may kings, established in their own duty, protect the earth forever;
and may this treatise on ethics remain for the mental satisfaction of the righteous like a newlywed bride.
May the Blessed One, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon, bring about the welfare of all people.
Separation of Friends.
Then the princes said: "Noble sir!"
"We have heard about the acquisition of friends;
now we wish to hear about the separation of friends.
Viṣṇuśarman said, "First, listen to the separation of friends."

Of this [work], the first verse is as follows: "The great and increasing affection between the lion and the bull in the forest was destroyed by a treacherous and excessively greedy jackal. (Hitopadeśa 2.1)
The princes asked, "How was that?
Viṣṇuśarman related: "In the Deccan region, there is a city named Suvarṇavatī. There dwells a merchant named Vardhamāna."

Although his wealth was abundant, seeing that his other relatives were even more prosperous, the thought occurred to him that he must further increase his riches. For it is said: "The greatness of one who looks downward only increases;
but all those who look upward become poor. (Hitopadeśa 2.2)
Furthermore:
Even a man who has killed a Brahmin is worthy of honor if he possesses abundant wealth; whereas one born of a lineage equal to the moon is held in contempt if he is destitute. (Hitopadeśa 2.3)
Furthermore:

Fortune does not desire to embrace one who lacks resolve, who is lazy, who relies solely on destiny, and who is suddenly devoid of effort—just as a young woman does not wish to embrace an old husband. (Hitopadeśa 2.4)
Furthermore:
Laziness, devotion to women, illness, attachment to one's native land, contentment, and cowardice—these six are obstacles to greatness. (Hitopadeśa 2.5)
For it is said:
"If one becomes conceited even with very little prosperity, I believe that Fate, considering its task accomplished, does not increase it further. (Hitopadeśa 2.6)
Furthermore:
"May no woman ever give birth to such a son—one who is devoid of enthusiasm, devoid of joy, devoid of vigor, and a source of delight for his enemies. (Hitopadeśa 2.7)
And so it has been said:

"One should seek to obtain what has not yet been obtained, protect with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (Hitopadeśa 2.8)
