For one who desires what has not yet been obtained, the acquisition of wealth is indeed the union with that object;

yet even for what has been obtained, if it is not protected, there is destruction even of a treasure. Moreover, wealth that does not increase, even if spent sparingly over time, goes to ruin like a medicinal ointment.
And if it is not being enjoyed, it is indeed useless;
as it has been said:
"Of what use is wealth to one who neither gives nor enjoys?"
Of what use is strength to one who does not subdue his enemies? Of what use is sacred learning to one who does not practice righteousness?
And of what use is a self to one who has not conquered his senses? (Hitopadeśa 2.9)
For it is said:
"Just as a jar is gradually filled by the falling of drops of water, that same principle is the cause of all branches of knowledge, of righteousness, and of wealth. (Hitopadeśa 2.10)
He whose days pass indeed devoid of both giving and enjoyment does not truly live, even though he breathes like a blacksmith's bellows. (Hitopadeśa 2.11)

Having reflected thus, he yoked two bulls named Nandaka and Sajīvaka to the pole, filled his cart with various kinds of goods, and set out toward Kaśmīra for trade. Furthermore: "Seeing the depletion of collyrium and the accumulation of an anthill, one should make the day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and work. (Hitopadeśa 2.12)
For it is said:
What is too heavy for the capable? What is too far for the persevering? What is a foreign land for the learned? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? (Hitopadeśa 2.13)
Then, as he was traveling, Sañjīvaka fell with a broken knee in a great forest named Sudurga.
Seeing him, Vardhamāna reflected:
"Though one who knows policy may indeed exert effort here and there,"
Furthermore, the fruit shall be exactly that which resides in the mind of the performer.
However—wonder is to be abandoned in every way, for it is an obstacle to all actions;
therefore, having cast aside wonder, let success be achieved in what is to be accomplished. (Hitopadeśa 2.15)
Having reflected thus, Vardhamāna abandoned Saṃjīvaka there; then, returning himself to the city named Dharmapura, he brought another bull of massive body, yoked him to the pole, and set out.
Thereupon, Saṃjīvaka also managed with great difficulty to rise up, bearing his weight upon his three hooves. For it is said:
Even for one submerged in a mass of water, fallen from a mountain,
or bitten by Takṣaka, life protects the vital organs.
A living being does not die before its time, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
yet one whose time has come does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
That which is unprotected remains if protected by destiny;
that which is well-protected perishes if struck down by destiny.
Even one abandoned in the forest without a protector lives, if favored by destiny.
Even though one has exerted every effort, one does not live at home forever.

Then, as the days passed, Saṃjīvaka, having taken his food and recreation according to his own will, wandered through the forest and roared mightily with his limbs robust and well-fed. In that forest lived a lion named Piṅgalaka, enjoying the happiness of a kingdom acquired by the strength of his own arms.
As it has been said:
No consecration or ritual refinement is performed for the lion by other beasts;
his sovereignty over the king of beasts is established of its own accord through the kingdom won by his prowess. (Hitopadeśa 2.19)
Once, overcome by thirst, he went to the bank of the Yamunā to drink water.
There, he heard Sañjīvaka’s bellowing, the likes of which he had never experienced before, sounding like the unseasonable thundering of a rain-cloud.
Upon hearing it, he did not drink the water; filled with alarm, he turned back, returned to his own place, and remained silent while reflecting, "What is this?"
He, being in such a state, was observed by his two ministers’ sons, Karaṭaka and Damanaka.
Seeing him in that condition, Damanaka said to Karaṭaka: "Friend Karaṭaka, why does our master stand here so startled and very slowly, though he is seeking water and has not yet drunk any?"
Karaṭaka said: "Friend Damanaka, in our opinion, service should not be rendered to him at all;
if that is the case, then what is the use to us of this investigation into our master's conduct?"

Since we have been long neglected by this king without cause, we have experienced great suffering. Behold what has been done by those servants who, desiring wealth through service, have lost even that independence of their own bodies, O fools! (Hitopadeśa 2.20)
Furthermore:

"The sufferings of cold, wind, and heat that those dependent on others endure—a wise person, having practiced austerity even to the extent of a fraction of those, shall become happy. (Hitopadeśa 2.21)
Moreover:
This much is the fulfillment of birth for embodied beings here among other embodied beings:
one should always practice what is beneficial with one's life, wealth, intellect, and speech. (Hitopadeśa 2.22)
Furthermore:
"Come here! Go away! Fall down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"—who has not been deceived by one whose eyes are like those of a startled deer? (Hitopadeśa 2.23)
Furthermore:
Like courtesans for the sake of gaining wealth, fools themselves repeatedly adorn their own selves and turn them into instruments for the benefit of others. (Hitopadeśa 2.24)
Furthermore:
Even the glance of a mistress, which is fickle by nature and falls even upon the impure, is highly esteemed by her servants. (Hitopadeśa 2.25)
Furthermore:
A fool may be silent, or one eloquent in speech may be a chatterer or a madman; if one does not endure out of fear, he is generally not of noble birth.
The bold one dwells by his side, while the timid remains at a distance;
the duty of service is exceedingly profound and inaccessible even to yogis. (Hitopadeśa 2.26)
And specifically:
"One bows down for the sake of advancement; one gives up one's life for the sake of livelihood;
one suffers for the sake of pleasure—who else is more foolish than a servant? (Hitopadeśa 2.27)
Damanaka said: "Friend, this must not be done by you even in thought under any circumstances;
for— Why indeed are the supreme lords not served with effort?
For when they are pleased, they fulfill one's desires in no time at all. (Hitopadeśa 2.28)
And furthermore:
Whence can those devoid of service obtain the splendor of the waving fly-whisks, the lofty white umbrella, or a procession of horses and elephants? (Hitopadeśa 2.29)
Karaṭaka said: "Nevertheless, what is the use of this business of ours?
For one must avoid involvement in matters that are not one's concern by all means. Observe:
'The man who desires to engage in activity regarding matters that are not his concern...'"
He alone goes to his destruction, like the monkey who pulled out the wedge.
Damanaka asks: "How was that? Karakaṭa relates:
Story 1.

In the land of Magadha, on ground adjacent to the Dharmāraṇya forest, a certain scribe named Śubhadatta had begun to construct a monastery. There, while a single pillar was being carved with a saw, a carpenter’s assistant drove a wedge into the middle of a split piece of wood that had been partially cleaved.
At that moment, a large troop of monkeys arrived, playing about.
A certain monkey, as if impelled by fate, sat down while grasping that wedge with both hands.
Immediately thereafter, out of his natural restlessness, he pulled at the wedge with great effort;
and once the wedge was pulled out, his two testicles were crushed and he met his death.
Therefore, I say: "To meddle in matters that are not one's concern," and so forth.
Damanaka said: "Nevertheless, a servant must certainly observe the movements of his master.
Karaṭaka said: "Let the chief minister, whoever has been appointed to every office, do it."
Therefore, a subordinate must never engage in discussion regarding the affairs of others. Observe:
"He who, out of a desire for his master's welfare, should discuss the affairs of others, will come to grief, just as a donkey does when struck because of its braying. (Hitopadeśa 2.31)
Damanaka asks: "How was that?
Karaṭaka says: "The second story."
In Vārāṇasī there was a washerman named Karpūrapaṭaka.
He fell into a deep sleep at night;
immediately thereafter, a thief entered to steal the goods from his house.
In his courtyard, a donkey stands tied up and a dog is sitting;
then the donkey says to the dog, "Friend!"
"This is indeed your duty;
so why do you not wake your master by making a loud noise?
The dog replied, "My good friend!"
"You must not question my instructions.
Do you not yourself know how I guard her house day and night?
For this man, having long since passed away, is unaware of my service."
Therefore, even now he shows little regard for providing me with food;
for without witnessing a calamity, masters become indifferent toward their dependents.
The donkey said: "Listen, you barbarian!"
He who makes a request at the time of need—is he a servant? Is he a friend?
A dog says:
"But he who addresses his servants only at the time of need—is he a master? (Hitopadeśa 2.32)
For it is said:
"In the maintenance of dependents, in service to a master, in the practice of dharma, and in the procreation of a son, there are no substitutes. (Hitopadeśa 2.33)
Then the donkey said with anger: "O you of wicked mind!
You are most sinful, since you show indifference toward the master's business in a time of calamity.
Let it be for now."
I must act in such a way that my master will remain awake; for it is said:
"One should serve the sun with one's back and the fire with one's belly."
One should serve one's master with one's whole being and with sincerity toward the next world.
Having said this, he let out an exceedingly loud braying sound.
Then the washerman, awakened by that braying, rose up in anger at the interruption of his sleep and struck the donkey with a cudgel;
by that, the donkey met its death.
Therefore, I say: "The discussion of another's office," and so forth.
Look, the very search for animals is our duty;
let the discussion of your own duty be carried out.
"But there is no need for that discussion today,
since we have plenty of food remaining from what we have already eaten.
Damanaka said with indignation, "How is it that you, seeking only food, serve the king alone?"
What you have said is incorrect; for:
[it arises] from the cause of benefiting friends and from the cause of harming even enemies.
Seeking the patronage of a king is desired by the wise;
who does not merely sustain his belly? (Hitopadeśa 2.35)
He whose life brings life to Brahmins, friends, and kinsmen—his life alone is fruitful; for who does not live for their own sake? (Hitopadeśa 2.36)
Moreover:
"He alone truly lives, by whose living many others live;
does not even a crow fill its own belly with its beak? (Hitopadeśa 2.37)
Behold:
some man falls into servitude for five ancient coins; another succeeds with a hundred thousand; yet another is not obtained even for a hundred thousand. (Hitopadeśa 2.38)
Furthermore:
Among the human race, which is equal for all, servitude is most contemptible; he who does not even consider that [servitude]—is he not counted among the living? (Hitopadeśa 2.39)
And so it has been said:
"The difference between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth;
and between women, men, and water is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth. (Hitopadeśa 2.40)
For indeed, even a very small amount excels [in its effect]:
having found a bone that is fleshless, filthy, and has only a trace of sinew and fat remaining, a dog attains satisfaction; yet it would not suffice to appease his hunger.
A lion slays an elephant even when abandoning a jackal that has come into its very lap;
indeed, every person, even when fallen into distress, desires a result commensurate with their own inner strength.
Furthermore, observe the difference between the master and the servant:
the wagging of the tail, the falling of the feet upon the ground, and the showing of the mouth and belly after prostrating.
A dog eats the morsel of food given by its master, while a noble elephant gazes steadfastly and partakes of it with hundreds of affectionate gestures.
Furthermore:
That life which is lived even for a moment by men renowned for their wisdom, prowess, and fame, and which remains unassailable—
Those who know the truth declare that such a life here is no life at all; even a crow lives for a long time and eats the offerings.
Furthermore:
He who shows no compassion toward his own son, nor toward his teacher, nor toward the circle of his servants, nor toward the destitute, nor toward his circle of kinsmen;
What is the fruit of such a life in the world of men?
Even a crow lives for a long time and consumes offerings. (Hitopadeśa 2.44)
Furthermore:
[He is] one whose intellect is devoid of discernment between the harmful and the beneficial,
and who has been excluded by many scriptural traditions.
What difference is there between a beast and a human beast whose sole desire is merely the filling of his belly? (Hitopadeśa 2.45)
Karaṭaka said, "We two are, after all, not the primary ministers;
so what is the use of this deliberation for us?
Damanaka replied, "In how much time do ministers attain preeminence or insignificance? For it is said:"
In this world, no one becomes noble or esteemed, nor indeed base or wicked, by virtue of their own inherent nature; rather,
it is through the influence of the world that one attains either the status of a teacher or the state of being its opposite.
It is one's own actions alone that lead a person [to their destination].
Furthermore:
Just as a stone is raised upon a mountain with great effort, yet is cast down in an instant, so too is the self [elevated or degraded] by virtues and faults. (Hitopadeśa 2.47)
A man goes lower and lower or rises higher by his own very actions, just like a digger of a well or a builder of a wall. (Hitopadeśa 2.48)
"That is auspicious;
for one's own self is indeed dependent upon one's own effort.
Karataka asked, "Then what do you say?"
He said, "This master Piṅgalaka has turned around and sat down out of some cause for alarm.
Karaṭaka replied, "A matter once uttered is understood even by beasts; horses and elephants carry their loads when urged."
Even what is unsaid, a wise person infers; for the fruit of intelligence is the knowledge of the gestures of others.
The mind within is discerned by the movements of the limbs, by the gait, by gestures, by speech, and by the expressions of the eyes and face. (Hitopadeśa 2.50)

In this matter of fear, by the power of my wisdom, I shall make this master my own. For: "He who knows how to speak words suited to the occasion, to give affection suited to true feeling, and to display anger suited to his own strength—he is a wise man. (Hitopadeśa 2.51)
Karaṭaka said: "Friend, you are ignorant of the ways of service. Behold:
'He who enters uninvited and speaks much without being asked, yet considers himself dear to the king—that man is of dull wit. (Hitopadeśa 2.52)
Damanaka said:
"My good sir, how am I unacquainted with service? Behold:
Is there anything that is beautiful or even unbeautiful by its very nature?"
Whatever pleases someone, that alone shall be beautiful to them.
For it is said:
"Whatever be the disposition of any person, by entering into that very disposition, a wise man should quickly bring that individual under his own control. (Hitopadeśa 2.54)
Furthermore:
"Who is here?"—to this one should reply, "It is I.
And when commanded, "Point the way correctly," one should carry out the king's command truthfully to the best of one's ability. (Hitopadeśa 2.55)
Furthermore:
One who has few desires, is steadfast, and wise, who always follows like a shadow, and does not waver when commanded—he may dwell in the king's residence. (Hitopadeśa 2.56)
Karaṭaka said: "Perhaps the master will take offense at your entering when it is not the proper occasion.
He replied: "Let it be so;
nevertheless, a dependent must certainly seek the presence of his master."
For it is said:
"To refrain from action out of fear of faults is the mark of a coward;
O brother, who would abandon food for fear of indigestion? (Hitopadeśa 2.57)
Behold—A king favors a man who is merely close at hand, even if he is devoid of learning, of low birth, or unknown.
Generally, lords of the earth and the creepers that are women alike entwine themselves around whoever dwells by their side. (Hitopadeśa 2.58)
Karaṭaka said, "Then, having gone there, what will you say?
He replied, "Listen. I shall find out whether my master is devoted to me or indifferent.
Karaṭaka asked, "What are the signs of that devotion?"

Damanaka said: "Listen—gazing from afar, laughter, great attentiveness when questioned, praising one's virtues even in one's absence, and remembering pleasant things [are signs of affection]. (Hitopadeśa 2.59)
Devotion toward one who does not serve, generosity, and pleasant speech—these are the signs of being devoted; even when a fault exists, one perceives it as a collection of virtues. (Hitopadeśa 2.60)
And furthermore:
"Delaying time, increasing hopes, and the destruction of results—a wise man should recognize these as the signs of one who has become indifferent to worldly power. (Hitopadeśa 2.61)
Having understood this, I shall speak in such a way that he will come under my control,
[describing] the calamity born from the vision of the miserable realms.
And the wise display the success born of the demonstration of skillful means, as if it were shimmering right before them, through the application of the methods of policy. (Hitopadeśa 2.62)
Karaṭaka said: "Even so, you ought not to speak when the occasion has not arrived;
for— 'Even Bṛhaspati, O Bhārata, by speaking words at an improper time, incurs contempt for his intelligence and suffers humiliation. (Hitopadeśa 2.63)
Damanaka said: "Friend, do not fear! I shall not speak a word until the proper occasion has arrived. For it is said:"

In times of calamity, when one has gone astray, or when there is a lapse in the timing of what must be done—even if unasked—one who seeks the welfare of others should speak words that are auspicious. (Hitopadeśa 2.64)
And if I am not to speak counsel even when the opportunity has arrived, then my very status as a counselor is untenable. For:
"That quality by which one maintains a livelihood and by which one is praised in the world must be protected and cultivated by the possessor of that quality. (Hitopadeśa 2.65)
"Therefore, my good friend, grant me leave; I am going. Karataka said, "May it be well with you; may your paths be auspicious."
"Let it be carried out as you desire.
Thereupon, Damanaka, as if filled with wonder, went into the presence of Piṅgalaka.
Then, from a distance, he was ushered in by the king with great respect; having prostrated himself with the eight-limbed salutation (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta*), he sat down.
The king said, "It has been a long time since you were last seen.

Damanaka replied, "Although there is no need for Your Majesty’s illustrious feet to have any concern with me, a servant, nevertheless, a subordinate must certainly present himself when the proper time arrives; thus, I have come. Furthermore—"
O King, even with a toothpick,
or by scratching the ear with a blade of grass, the needs of lords are accomplished.
What need has a man who possesses limbs, speech, and hands? // Hit_2.66 //
Even though it may be possible for my intellect to perish because I have been neglected by Your Majesty for a long time,
that too should not be suspected; for even one whose conduct is characterized by fortitude, though he be treated with contempt—
The destruction of the intellect is not to be feared;
for even when cast downward, the flame of fire never goes below. (Hitopadeśa 2.67)
"Your Majesty, a master must in every way be a discerning judge; for— 'A gem rolls at one's feet, while glass is worn upon the head.
Let glass remain as glass and the gem as a gem, exactly as they are. (Hitopadeśa 2.68)
Furthermore:
When a king behaves without distinction, treating everyone equally, then the enthusiasm of those capable of exertion declines. (Hitopadeśa 2.69)
Moreover: "O King, there are three kinds of men—superior, inferior, and middling;
one should employ them accordingly in three corresponding types of tasks. (Hitopadeśa 2.70)
For it is said:
Servants and ornaments are both to be employed only in their proper places;
for a crest-jewel is not worn on the foot, nor is an anklet placed upon the head. (Hitopadeśa 2.71)
Moreover:
If a gem fit for gold ornaments is set in tin, it neither cries out nor fails to shine; rather, the blame falls upon the one who employed it. (Hitopadeśa 2.72)
And furthermore:
A piece of glass set in a crown, and a gem in an anklet—there is no fault in the gem, but rather the ignorance of the noble person. (Hitopadeśa 2.73)
Behold:
"This one is wise and loyal; this one is brave; here lies danger"—thus, a king who understands how to evaluate his servants is surrounded by them. (Hitopadeśa 2.74)
For instance:
a horse, a weapon, a scripture, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—having encountered a particular person, they become either unworthy or worthy. (Hitopadeśa 2.75)
Moreover:
"What is the use of one who is devoted but incapable, or one who is capable but harmful?
O King, you ought not to disregard me, for I am both devoted and capable. (Hitopadeśa 2.76)
For this reason:
through the king's contempt, the retinue becomes devoid of intelligence;
consequently, because of that [retinue's] authority, wise men do not remain in his presence.
When the kingdom is abandoned by the wise, policy does not become virtuous;
when policy has failed, the entire world, being powerless, perishes.
Furthermore:
People always honor one who is honored by the king;
but he who is held in contempt by the king is despised by everyone. (Hitopadeśa 2.78)
Furthermore, it has been said by the wise: "One should accept even from a child that which is spoken with reason;
for is there not the illumination of a lamp even within the range of the sun? (Hitopadeśa 2.79)
Piṅgalaka said: "My dear Damanaka, what is this? You are the son of our chief minister; for so long a time you have not come from anywhere due to the words of wicked men.
Now, speak as you please."
Damanaka said: "Your Majesty, I wish to ask something;
let it be spoken."
The master, seeking water, stood as if astonished, not having drunk even a drop.
Piṅgalaka said, "You have spoken well;
however, there is no one who is a fit ground for confidence to whom I may tell this secret."
Nevertheless, I shall speak to you in confidence;
listen. At present, this forest is inhabited by extraordinary beings, and therefore it must be abandoned by us.
For this reason, I am filled with wonder.
"And likewise, I too have heard a great and unprecedented sound;
according to this sound, this creature must possess great strength.
Damanaka said, "O King!"

Indeed, this is a great cause for fear; that sound was heard even by her. But is he truly a minister who first abandons his post and only afterwards engages in battle? In such a matter of doubt regarding duty, the utility of servants must indeed be examined. For it is said:
On the touchstone of adversity, a man learns the true worth of his circle of kinsmen, women, and servants, as well as the integrity of his own intellect and character. (Hitopadeśa 2.80)
The lion said, "My good sir,
a great fear afflicts me.
Damanaka replied to himself, "Otherwise, why do you speak to me of abandoning the pleasures of sovereignty to go to another place?"
Prakāśa said aloud: "O King, as long as I live, you need not fear;
however, Karaṭaka and the others should also be reassured, for at the time of countering a calamity, a gathering of men is difficult to find."
Then Damanaka and Karaṭaka, having been honored by the king with his entire wealth and having pledged to counteract the danger, set out.

As they were walking along, Karaṭaka said to Damanaka: "Friend, how was this great favor accepted after pledging to pacify the danger without first ascertaining whether the cause of fear could be countered through one's own power or was beyond the reach of remedy?"

For one who provides no service should not accept a gift from anyone, especially from a king. Behold: "In whose favor dwells Fortune, in whose prowess dwells victory, and in whose anger dwells death—he indeed is composed of all splendor. (Hitopadeśa 2.81)
For thus it is said:
"A king must not be despised even if he is a child, for thinking 'he is but a man'; for he is a great deity abiding in human form. (Hitopadeśa 2.82)
Damanaka laughed and said, "Friend,
remain silent;
I have discovered the cause of your fear."
That is merely the bellowing of a bull;
bulls are food for us as well,
so what need is there to mention a lion?
Karaṭaka said: "If this is so, then why was the fear of the master not removed right there?

Damanaka replied: "If the fear of the master were released right there, how could this great gain of favor have occurred? Furthermore, a master should never be treated with indifference by his servants."
Having made his master indifferent, a servant should act like Dadhikarṇa.
Karaṭaka asked, "How was that? Damanaka related:
Story 3.
In the northern region, on a mountain named Arbudaśikhara, there lived a lion of great prowess named Durdānta.
While he was reclining in a mountain cave, a certain mouse would daily gnaw off the tips of his mane.
Seeing the tips of his mane thus cut, the lion became enraged; however, being unable to find the mouse within its hole, he thought:
If there is a petty enemy who cannot be overcome by valor alone, one should place a soldier equal to him in front to strike him down. (Hitopadeśa 2.84)
Having reflected thus, he went to the village, gained the cat's trust, and after bringing a cat named Dadhikarṇa with great care and giving him meat to eat, he placed him in his own cave.
Thereafter, out of fear of that cat, the mouse also no longer emerged from its hole;
thus, the lion slept happily with his mane unharmed.
Whenever he heard the sound of a mouse,
he would nourish that cat by giving it meat.
To disobey the commands of kings and to show disrespect toward brahmins— these two lead to ruin.
Sleeping separately from women is a death not brought about by weapons.
Then Saṃjīvaka, unacquainted with the local customs, approached Karakaṭaka in fear and prostrated before him with the eight-limbed salutation (*aṣṭāṅga-pāta*).
As it has been said:
"Intelligence alone is more powerful than physical strength; for in its absence, this is the fate that awaits elephants."
Thus does the drum, struck by the elephant-keeper and resounding, seem to proclaim this. (Hitopadeśa 2.86)
Then Saṃjīvaka said with apprehension: "General, what must I do?
Let that be told."
Karaṭaka said: "O bull, you are staying here in this forest;
pay homage to the lotus-feet of our lord."
Saṃjīvaka said, "Then grant me the word of safety; I shall go.
Karaṭaka said, "Listen, you bull! Enough of this apprehension; for— [Verse follows]"
Keśava gave no reply to the Cedi king who was cursing him;
for a lion does not echo the howl of a jackal, nor does it respond to the cries of a vulture.
And furthermore:
The wind does not uproot the soft grasses that lie low and bend in every direction.
A great man strikes down only those trees that are tall; he displays his prowess only against the mighty.
Then, having placed Sañjīvaka at a certain distance away, the two went into the presence of Piṅgalaka.
Thereupon, the king looked upon them with respect; they bowed and sat down.
The king said, "Was he seen by you?"
Damanaka said: "Your Majesty, he has been seen;
however, that which Your Majesty has understood is indeed so."
"He is indeed a great man who wishes to see the King;
however, since he possesses great strength, let him wait while you prepare yourself.
One should not be afraid of mere sound."
And so it has been said:
"One should not be afraid of mere words without understanding the cause of those words;
having fully understood the cause of the words, the procuress attained respect. (Hitopadeśa 2.89)
The king asked, "How was that? Damanaka related: Story 4.
In the midst of Śrīparvata, there is a city named Brahmapura.
It is commonly reported among the people that a rākṣasa named Ghaṇṭākarṇa dwells on its summit.
Once, a certain thief who was fleeing while carrying a bell was killed by a tiger.
The bell that had fallen from his hand was seized by the monkeys;
the monkeys rang that bell at every moment.
Consequently, the city folk saw that man being devoured while the sound of the bell was heard at every instant.

Immediately thereafter, it was said that Ghaṇṭākarṇa, being enraged, was devouring men and ringing his bell; having heard this, all the people fled from the city. Then, a procuress named Karālā reflected, "This sound of the bell is not inferior; could it be that monkeys are ringing the bell? Having thus understood for herself, she informed the king: "O King!"
"If some expenditure of wealth is made, then I shall subdue this Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
Thereupon, the king gave her the money.

The procuress prepared a ritual circle (*maṇḍala*), displayed there the solemnity of worshiping Gaṇeśa and the other deities, and having herself taken fruits dear to monkeys, she entered the forest and scattered the fruits about.
Then, leaving the bell behind, the monkeys became intent upon the fruits;
the procuress, taking the bell, returned to the city and became honored by all the people.
Therefore I say: "One should not fear mere sounds," and so forth.
Then, having brought Sañjīvaka there, they allowed him to see them;
thereafter, he lived right there in the greatest joy.
Then once, a lion named Stabdha-karṇa, the brother of that lion, arrived.
Having offered him hospitality and seated the lion, Piṅgalaka set out to kill an animal for his meal.
In the meantime, Saṃjīvaka said: "O King!"
"Where are the meats of the deer killed today? The King said, "Damanaka and Karaṭaka know. Saṃjīvaka replied, "Let it be found out whether there is any or not."
The lion reflected and said, "That is simply not possible.
Saṃjīvaka asked, "How could so much meat have been eaten by those two? The king replied, "It was eaten, spent, and even discarded."
This was the daily routine.
Saṃjīvaka asked, "How is it being done out of the very sight of Your Majesty’s illustrious feet?
The king replied, "It is being done precisely out of my sight."
Then Saṃjīvaka said: "This is not proper.
And so it has been said:
'One should not do anything on one's own initiative without having informed one's master.'"
O Lord of the World, there is no task other than the remedying of calamities.
Moreover:
O King, a minister who gives little but takes much is like a water-pot; a fool is like a girdle-bell; and one who is poor is like a single cowrie shell. (Hitopadeśa 2.91)
For that minister is always superior who increases even a single kākini;
for one who possesses a treasury, the treasury is his life, whereas for a king, life itself is not merely life.
Furthermore, a man does not attain service through wealth or family traditions;
one who is destitute of riches is abandoned even by his own wife, let alone by others. (Hitopadeśa 2.93)
And this is the primary fault of a king:

excessive expenditure, lack of foresight, as well as acquisition through unrighteous means, and the plundering of those situated at a distance—this is called the ruin of the treasury. (Hitopadeśa 2.94)
For it is said:

"One who spends according to his own desires without considering quickly what is long-term and what is extensive will surely be exhausted, even if he is a wealthy man equal to Vaiśravaṇa. (Hitopadeśa 2.95)

Stabdha-karṇa said: "Listen, brother! These two, Damanaka and Karaṭaka, who have long been our dependents and are currently authorized for matters of peace and war, should never be appointed to positions of financial authority.
Furthermore, regarding the matter of appointment, I shall relate what I have heard:
'A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a relative is not recommended for a position of authority.'"
A Brahmin does not give away even a proven object, even with great difficulty.
An appointed Kṣatriya certainly brandishes his sword over wealth;
a kinsman, having assailed one through the pretense of kinship, seizes all one's possessions.
Even when he has committed an offense, a long-serving official remains fearless;
disregarding his master, he acts without restraint. (Hitopadeśa 2.98)
One who holds a position of authority and acts as a benefactor does not perceive his own transgression;
making his very service a banner, he plunders everything. (Hitopadeśa 2.99)
Since a minister who plays in secret becomes like a king himself, he will certainly always treat [the king] with contempt due to familiarity. (Hitopadeśa 2.100)
"One who is inwardly corrupt yet outwardly patient causes all manner of misfortune;
Śakuni and Śakaṭāra are the two examples of this, O King. (Hitopadeśa 2.101)
For indeed, every minister who is prosperous would be impossible to manage;
this is the instruction of the perfected ones: prosperity is a corruption of the mind. (Hitopadeśa 2.102)
Failing to grasp the purpose at hand, misappropriating state property, acting out of favoritism, indifference, and lack of intelligence—these are the vices of a minister. (Hitopadeśa 2.103)

The means for a king to grasp the true nature of his officials consists of constant examination, the granting of rewards according to their conduct, and likewise the reversal of their duties when necessary. (Hitopadeśa 2.104)
When oppressed, officials generally vomit up the very essence of the king, like malignant ulcers; for such indeed is the nature of those in office. (Hitopadeśa 2.105)
O Lord of the Earth, the stream of wealth should be constrained only occasionally;
does a bathing garment, once wrung out, ever release the water it has held? (Hitopadeśa 2.106)
Having understood all this according to the proper occasion, one should act accordingly.
The lion said, "That may well be so;
however, these two do not carry out my commands in any way."
Stabdhakarṇa said: "All of this is entirely improper;
for— 'A king should not tolerate even his own sons who violate his commands.
What indeed is the difference between a king and a king depicted in a painting? (Hitopadeśa 2.107)"
The fame of the stubborn perishes; friendship perishes for the poisonous; the family of one whose senses are lost perishes; the virtue of one intent on wealth perishes;
the fruit of knowledge for the addicted perishes; and the happiness of the miser perishes.
The kingdom of a lord of men whose ministers are negligent.
Furthermore:
A king should protect his subjects like a father from thieves, from appointed officials, from enemies, from those favored by the king, and from his own greed. (Hitopadeśa 2.109)
"Brother, by all means let our word be followed. The legal transaction has already been completed by us:
let this Sañjīvaka, who consumes the grain, be appointed to the office of steward."
When it was carried out according to these words, from that time forth, Piṅgalaka and Sañjīvaka passed their time with great affection, having abandoned all other kinsmen.
Then, observing a slackening even in the provision of food for the attendants, Damanaka and Karaṭaka began to deliberate with one another.
Damanaka said to Karaṭaka: "Friend!"
What is to be done? This fault was committed by oneself;
even regarding a fault committed by oneself, lamentation is improper.
And so it has been said:
"Having touched the gold line and bound herself, the messenger;
and the virtuous man wishing to seize the jewel—these are all made miserable by their own faults. (Hitopadeśa 2.110)
Karaṭaka asks: "How was that? Damanaka relates:
Story 5.
In a city named Kāñcanapura, there was a king called Vīravikrama.

While a certain barber was being led by the king’s magistrate to the place of execution, a wandering mendicant named Kandarpaketu, accompanied by a virtuous companion, cried out, "He must not be killed! and seized him by the hem of his garment.
The king’s men said, "Why should he not be put to death?
He replied, "Listen;
having touched Svarṇarekhā," and so forth, he recited.
They asked, "How was this?
The wandering mendicant related: "I am named Darpaketu, the son of King Jīmūtaketu of Siṃhaladvīpa.

On the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, beneath a manifested wish-granting tree (*kalpataru*), I saw a maiden seated upon a couch of white lotuses shimmering with the rays of a jeweled necklace, adorned with every ornament, playing the lute like Lakṣmī herself."
"A certain woman is seen. Thereupon, I took a merchant from a ship, boarded the vessel, and went there.
Having arrived there, I beheld her seated upon a couch in that very same manner.
Then, drawn by the quality of her beauty, I too leapt after her.
Immediately thereafter, having reached the City of Gold (*kanakapattana*), I beheld her seated upon a couch in a golden palace, attended by Vidyādharīs;
nevertheless, seeing me from afar, she dispatched a female friend and addressed me with great courtesy.
And when I was questioned by her friend, she related this: "This is Ratnamañjarī by name, the daughter of the Vidyādhara emperor named Kandarpakeli,
who has made a vow that whoever comes and beholds Kanakavartana with their own eyes [shall be his wife]."
The mental resolve was: "He himself, though beyond my father's reach, will marry me.
Therefore, may you marry her by the Gāndharva rite.
Once that Gāndharva marriage has taken place, I shall remain there, sporting with her.
Then, on one occasion, she said to him in private: "My lord, all this may be enjoyed according to your will;
however, this Vidyādharī named Svarṇarekhā, who is depicted here in a painting, must never be touched."
Thereafter, curiosity having arisen within me, I touched Suvarṇarekhā with my own hand;
yet, being struck by her lotus-foot even though she was but a painting, I fell back into my own kingdom.
Then, distressed, I went forth as a wandering mendicant and, while roaming the earth, arrived at this city.
And here, on the following day, while sleeping in the cowherd’s house, I saw this:
at the time of dusk, having finished tending the cattle, the cowherd returned to his own home and saw his wife consulting with a female messenger.
Thereupon, having beaten that cowherd-woman and bound her to a pillar, he went to sleep.

Then, at midnight, the messenger—the bride of that barber—approached the cowherd woman again and said: "He is as if on the verge of death, consumed by the fire of separation from you and shattered by the arrows of Love.
And so it is said:
"When the darkness has been dispelled by the Lord of Night..."
The god of love pierced the hearts of the youths again and again upon seeing her.
Having observed his condition to be such, I have come with a distressed mind to attend upon you;
therefore, I remain here having bound myself.
You should go there, gratify him, and return quickly.
When this had been carried out, the cowherd woke up and said, "Now I shall lead you, most wicked woman, into the presence of your lover.
When she did not say anything at all in response, the cowherd became enraged and said, "Out of pride, you do not even give me an answer to my words," and in his anger,
he took a knife and cut off her nose.
Having done so, the cowherd fell asleep once more and entered into slumber.
Then the cowherd woman arrived and asked her messenger, "What is the news?
The messenger replied, "Look at me."
The face itself tells the story.
Immediately thereafter, that cowherd woman, having done so, remained there bound. And this messenger, taking her with her severed nose, entered her own home and stayed there.

Then, early in the morning, when this barber was asked for his wife's shaving kit, he gave her only a single razor. Because the kit was incomplete, the barber became enraged and threw that razor from a distance right into the house. Then, crying out, "He has cut off my nose with this! she brought him before the magistrate.
And that cowherd woman, being questioned again by that cowherd, said: "O wicked one!
