That swan, your king, is entirely too soft."
He has no authority over the kingdom; since he is so utterly weak that he is unable to protect even an object held in the palm of his hand, how can he rule the earth?
What does his kingdom matter to you? You are like a frog in a well; therefore, you teach based on that [limited] perspective. Listen:
One should resort to a great tree endowed with both fruit and shade;
even if by fate there is no fruit, by whom can the shade be withheld? (Hitopadeśa 3.10)
And furthermore:
One should not serve the lowly; one should rely upon the great.
Even milk, when in the hand of a liquor-seller, is called *vāruṇī*. (Hitopadeśa 3.11)
Furthermore:

Even a vast expansion of virtues becomes diminished when residing in one devoid of merit, due to the relationship between the container and the contained, like a lordly elephant reflected in a mirror. (Hitopadeśa 3.12)
But—by the grace of the lion, the goat wanders fearlessly in the forest;
having approached Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa obtained the kingdom in Laṅkā. (Hitopadeśa 3.13)
And specifically:
"Success may be achieved even through mere designation when the lord of men possesses great power;
by the designation of 'hare,' rabbits dwell in comfort under the moon. (Hitopadeśa 3.14)
I asked, "How was that?
The birds related the story—
Story 3.
Once, even during the rainy season, due to a lack of rain, a herd of elephants afflicted by thirst said to their leader: "O Lord, what means is there for our survival?
There is not even a place for small creatures to submerge themselves."
"And we, having no place to plunge into, are as good as dead; like the blind, what shall we do? Where shall we go?
Then the elephant king, having gone not very far, showed them a clear lake.
Then, as the days passed, the small rabbits dwelling on that bank were crushed by the blows of the elephants' feet.
Thereupon, a rabbit named Śilīmukha reflected: "This herd of elephants, distressed by thirst, must come here every day;
consequently, our family will be destroyed."
Then an old hare named Vijaya said, "Do not despair;
I shall provide a remedy for this.
Having thus made his promise, he departed.
As he was going, he reflected: "How can I speak while standing in the presence of the leader of the elephant herd? For it is said:
'An elephant kills even by touching; a serpent kills even by smelling;
a king harms even while protecting; and a wicked person injures even while laughing. (Hitopadeśa 3.15)
Therefore, having climbed to the mountain peak, I shall speak with the leader of the herd.
When this had been done, the leader of the herd said: "Who are you?
From where have you come?"
He said, "I am a hare.
I have been sent into your presence by the Blessed Moon.
The leader of the herd said, "State your business."
Vijaya said:
"Even when weapons are raised, a messenger speaks not otherwise; for, by virtue of his perpetual immunity from harm, he is a speaker of the truth. (Hitopadeśa 3.16)
Therefore, by his command, I speak; listen.
That these rabbits, the guardians of the Moon-lake, were driven out by you was an improper act;
those rabbits have been protected by us for a long time.
"For this very reason, I am renowned as Śaśāṅka.
When the messenger had spoken thus, the leader of the herd, out of fear, said this:
"O spy, this was done through ignorance."
"I will not go there again.
The messenger said, "If that is so, then having bowed to the Blessed Moon, who is trembling with anger here in this lake, and having propitiated him, you may depart."
Then, having led the leader of the herd there at night and shown him the shimmering reflection of the moon in that water, he caused the leader of the herd to prostrate; and he said:
"O Lord!"
"This offense was committed by him out of ignorance;
therefore, let it be forgiven. He will not act in this way again."
Having said this, he was sent away.
Therefore, we say: "Success would be achieved even through mere designation.
Then I said: "That very King Haṃsa, our lord, is of great majesty and exceedingly wise."
"Even sovereignty over the three worlds would be appropriate for him there, let alone a kingdom.
Then I was addressed by those birds: "O wicked one!"
Having been asked, "How is it that you roam in our realm? he was led into the presence of King Citravarna.
Then, having presented me before the king, they bowed and said, "O Lord, please listen."
"This wicked man, though wandering in our own country, insults Your Majesty's feet.
The king asked, "Who is this? From where has he come?"
They said: "I am a follower of the royal swan named Hiraṇyagarbha, come from Karpūradvīpa. Then I was asked by the vulture minister, 'Who is the chief minister there?
I replied, 'A ruddy goose named Sarvajña, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.'"
The vulture said: "It is appropriate;
he is born of our own land. For:
One who is born in one's own country, pure in family conduct, and proven honest through tests..."
One who knows the mantras, is homeless, and is free from transgression. // Hit_3.17 //
The king should appoint as a minister one who has studied the meaning of legal procedures, who is of noble birth, renowned, wise, and a producer of wealth. (Hitopadeśa 3.18)
In the meantime, Śuka said: "O King, the minor islands such as Karpūra-dvīpa and others are indeed included within Jambūdvīpa;
even there, O King, your majesty alone holds sovereign authority."
Then the king also said: "It is exactly so;
for— A king, one intoxicated, a child, a woman, and one proud of wealth—these desire even that which is unattainable, let alone that which is already obtainable. (Hitopadeśa 3.19)
Then I said: "If sovereignty is established by mere words alone, then our lord Hiraṇyagarbha also possesses ownership over Jambūdvīpa. Śuka asked: "How is the decision to be made in this matter?"
I said, "Only in battle.
The king laughed and said, "Go to your own master and prepare him.
Then I said, "Let your own messenger also be dispatched."
The king said: "Who will go on this mission as an envoy? For an envoy must be of such a nature: devoted, virtuous, pure, skillful, eloquent, free from vices, and patient."
A Brahmin who knows the vital secrets of others should be the envoy, being endowed with ready wit.
The vulture said: "There are indeed many messengers, but a Brahmin alone should be appointed. For it is said:
'She shows favor to her husband and does not covet wealth.'"
The blackness of the *kālakūṭa* poison does not depart even through contact with the Lord.
The king said: "In that case, let Śuka go himself.
Śuka, you yourself must go there with him and speak our desire."
The parrot said, "As Your Majesty commands;
however, this crane is a wicked person.
Therefore, I will not go with him."
And so it has been said:
"The wicked man commits an evil deed, yet its fruit surely falls upon the virtuous;
Rāvaṇa abducted Sītā, but the binding was that of the great ocean. (Hitopadeśa 3.22)
Furthermore:
One should never remain nor go anywhere with a wicked person; for through association with a crow, the swan was killed while standing, and the quail while walking. (Hitopadeśa 3.23)
The king said: "How was that? Śuka relates:
Story 4.
On the outskirts of the road to Ujjayinī, there was a Plakṣa tree where a swan and a crow lived.
Once, during the summer season, a certain weary traveler, having placed his bow and arrow beneath that tree, fell asleep.
Then, in another moment, the shadow of the tree moved away from his face.
Seeing his face then enveloped by the heat of the sun,
the virtuous and pure royal swan, who was perched upon that tree, out of compassion spread his wings and once again cast a shadow over his face.
Then, a traveler who was exhausted from wandering the road and enjoying a deep sleep opened his mouth.
Thereupon, that crow, unable to endure the happiness of another due to his innate wickedness, voided excrement into his mouth and fled.
Then, as soon as that traveler rose and looked upward—
At that moment, the swan was spotted by him, struck with an arrow, and killed.
Therefore I say: "One should not remain [in a place].
O King, I shall also tell the story of the quail; please listen.
Story 5:
A crow and a quail lived happily together in a single tree.
Once, on the occasion of a festival for the Lord Garuḍa, all the birds went to the seashore.
Then the quail set out together with the crow.
As they were going along, the crow repeatedly ate the curd from the vessel placed upon the head of a cowherd.
Thereupon, when the cowherd set the curd-vessel on the ground and looked up,
Then he saw a crow and a quail. Upon seeing him, the crow fled; but the quail, being by nature innocent and slow of movement, was overtaken and killed by him.
Therefore I said, "One must not go," and so forth.
Then I asked, "Brother Śuka, why do you speak thus?"
"As Śrīmad-deva-pāda is toward me, so too are you.
Śuka said: "Let it be so;
however, even those things which are agreeable and pleasing when spoken by the wicked—"
For they indeed produce fear, like flowers out of season.
And your wickedness has been understood from your very words, since your speech alone was the cause for the conflict between these two kings. Behold:
even when a fault has been committed before his eyes, a fool is satisfied with mere conciliation.
The chariot-maker placed his own wife, together with her paramour, upon his head.
The king asked, "How was that? Śuka relates:
Story 6.
In the city of Yauvanaśrī, there was a wheelwright named Mandamati.
He knew his own wife to be unchaste; however, he did not see her with his own eyes in one place together with her paramour.
Then that chariot-maker, having said, "I am going to another village," set out. After traveling some distance, he returned and remained hidden in his own house upon his couch.
Then, believing that the chariot-maker had gone to another village, the lover arrived at the very time of twilight, feeling confident.
Afterwards, while she was sporting intensely with that lover upon that couch,
she realized through the touch of a certain limb that her husband was lying on the surface of the couch was a magician;
thereupon, she became despondent in her mind.
Then the lover said, "Why do you not enjoy yourself fully with me today?
You appear to me as if you are astonished.
Thereupon she replied, "You are ignorant [of this]."
That lord of my life,
with whom I have been friends since childhood— he has gone to another village today;
without him, even this village filled with all the people appears to me like a wilderness.
"What will happen? What did he eat in that other place?
Or how did he fall asleep?"—thus our hearts are torn asunder.
The lover said, "Is this kind of chariot-maker such an object of your affection? The unchaste woman replied, "O barbarian!
What are you saying? Listen—"
That woman who, even when addressed with harsh words or looked upon with eyes of anger by her husband, maintains a serene countenance, is a vessel for righteousness.
Furthermore:
Whether dwelling in a city or in a forest, whether wicked or pure—if a husband is dear to women, their worlds will be of great prosperity. (Hitopadeśa 3.27)
And furthermore:
"For a husband is a woman's supreme ornament, even without other ornaments;
deprived of him, she does not shine, however beautiful she may be. (Hitopadeśa 3.28)
And you are a paramour of evil intent; due to the fickleness of the mind, you are sometimes served like a flower or betel nut, and sometimes not served at all.
Moreover, that master of mine intends to sell me to the gods.
Or he is capable of giving [his wealth] to the Brahmins.
What more need be said? While he lives, I live;
and upon his death, I shall follow him in death—such is the vow I maintain. For it is said:
For as many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
one who follows her husband shall dwell in heaven for that long.
Moreover:
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too, by taking her husband [with her], she is glorified in the heavenly world. (Hitopadeśa 3.30)
Furthermore:
"For that beloved woman who, having embraced her unconscious husband on the funeral pyre, abandons her own body,"
Even if one has committed a hundred thousand sins,
by taking hold of her husband, such a person shall attain the world of the gods.
For it is said:
To whomsoever her father gives her, or her brother with the father’s consent, she should serve him while he lives and must not disregard him when he has passed away. (Hitopadeśa 3.32)
Having heard all this, that dull-witted carpenter thought to himself, "Blessed am I,
whose wife speaks so kindly and is so devoted to her husband," and placing that bed,
along with the man and woman, upon his head, he danced with joy.
Therefore, I say: "Even when a fault has been committed before one's eyes," and so forth.
Consequently, I was honored by that king according to custom and sent on my way;
Śuka also followed behind me.
"Having understood all of this, let it be considered what ought to be done.
The Cakravāka laughed and said, "O King,
the Baka has already traveled to another land and performed the king's business to the best of his ability."
But, O King, this is the very nature of fools; for:
"One should give a hundred [coins] rather than quarrel"—this is the consensus of the wise.
To engage in conflict even without cause is the characteristic of a fool. (Hitopadeśa 3.33)
The king said, "Enough with this reproaching of the past; let us attend to the matter at hand. The cakravāka bird replied, "Your Majesty," [and continued].

I speak this in solitude; for the wise can infer the mind even from complexion, form, and echoes, as well as from changes in the eyes and face; therefore, one should deliberate in secret. (Hitopadeśa 3.34)
Then the king and the minister remained there while the others went elsewhere.
The cakravāka said: "Your Majesty, I know this for certain: this was carried out by the crane at the instigation of one of our own servants. For: [Verse follows]"
Among those who possess objects of knowledge, the sick man is better; among officials, the one in distress;
among the learned, the fool; and among the virtuous, the one of noble birth is the best support for life. (Hitopadeśa 3.35)
The king said, "Let it be;
the cause for this shall be investigated later. For now, let that which must be done be determined."
The ruddy goose said:
"Your Majesty, let a vow first be made regarding that matter;
then we shall know how to carry it out and what our strength and weakness may be. For instance:"
In observing what ought and ought not to be done within one's own kingdom and those of others, the spy is the eye of the ruler; he who lacks such a spy is truly blind.
And he should take a second person worthy of trust and let him go;
having himself remained there, he should determine the secret plan for that place thoroughly and, having informed the second person, send him away.
And so it has been said:
"For the sake of the Teacher’s wisdom, one should dwell together with one's own spies, who are endowed with the appearance of ascetics, at sacred fords, hermitages, or temples. (Hitopadeśa 3.37)
And as for the one who moves secretly both in water and on land,
let that very crane be appointed;
let some crane exactly like him go as a second.
And let the householders of that house stand at the king's gate; however, even this must be carried out with great secrecy. For:
"A secret counsel is betrayed by six ears, as is news once it has reached its destination."
Thus, the king should act with himself as his only companion. (Hitopadeśa 3.38)
Behold:
"For those faults that arise for a lord of the earth from the disclosure of counsel cannot be remedied; such is the opinion of those who know the science of policy. (Hitopadeśa 3.39)
The king reflected and said, "I have indeed obtained an excellent substitute. The minister replied, "Your Majesty,
victory in battle has also been obtained."
In the meantime, the doorkeeper entered, bowed, and said:
"Your Majesty, a parrot has arrived from Jambudvīpa and stands at the gate. The king looked toward the cakravāka.
The Cakravāka said, "Let him go and stay for now while he establishes his residence; later, having brought him here, he shall be seen.
Having replied, "As Your Majesty commands," the doorkeeper took the parrot and went to that place of residence.
The king said, "War is now imminent.
The Cakravāka replied, "O King, even so, war should certainly not be undertaken first. For it is said:"
Is he a servant? Is he a minister? He who, at the very outset, advises the king on military exertion and the abandonment of his own territory without due deliberation. (Hitopadeśa 3.40)
Furthermore:
One should strive to conquer enemies never by means of war, because victory is seen to be uncertain for two parties engaged in combat. (Hitopadeśa 3.41)
Furthermore:
One should strive to subdue enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension—either collectively or individually—but never by means of war. (Hitopadeśa 3.42)
Furthermore:
Indeed, every person is a hero so long as they have not encountered combat;
for who would not be filled with pride when the prowess of an opponent has not yet been witnessed? (Hitopadeśa 3.43)
Furthermore:
A stone is not raised by living beings as easily as wood;
great accomplishment through small means—this is the great fruit of this mantra. (Hitopadeśa 3.44)
However, seeing that war has arrived, let us act; for—as it is said:
"Just as agriculture becomes fruitful through effort made at the proper time, so too, O King, this policy bears fruit after a long time, not in an instant. (Hitopadeśa 3.45)
Furthermore: Fearfulness when far away and courage when near is a great quality;
for in this world, it is the truly great person who attains steadfastness in the face of calamity. (Hitopadeśa 3.46)
And furthermore:
"It is said that the first obstacle to all accomplishments is zeal;
does not even extremely cold water split mountains? (Hitopadeśa 3.47)
"There is no precedent for fighting with one who is stronger;
such a battle with an elephant would bring death to men. (Hitopadeśa 3.48)
Moreover:
He is a fool who, having reached the wrong time, engages with an enemy; it is like a quarrel with one more powerful, or like the emergence of wings on a worm. (Hitopadeśa 3.49)
Furthermore:
Adopting the contraction of a tortoise, one should endure even a blow;
but when the time is right, a knower of policy should rise up like a fierce serpent. (Hitopadeśa 3.50)
One who knows the proper means is equally capable of uprooting great things as small ones;
just as the current of a river uproots trees as easily as blades of grass. (Hitopadeśa 3.51)
Therefore, let this parrot, our messenger, be detained here for the time being while the fortress is prepared; for:
"A single archer standing upon the rampart can fight off a hundred; a hundred can fight off ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is of superior importance. (Hitopadeśa 3.52)
Furthermore:
To whom is a kingdom without a fortress not a source of humiliation for an enemy?
A king without a fortress is without refuge, like a man fallen from a ship. (Hitopadeśa 3.53)
One should construct a fortress with a great moat, provided with high walls, equipped with mechanical engines and water, and situated near mountains, rivers, deserts, or forests. (Hitopadeśa 3.54)

Extensive extent, lack of unevenness, the storage of liquids, grain, and firewood, the ability to enter, and the presence of water-supplies—these seven are the excellences of a fortress. (Hitopadeśa 3.55)
The king said, "Who should be appointed to investigate the fortress?
The cakravāka replied,
"One should employ in a task that person who is skilled in it."
One who has not experienced the results of karma becomes bewildered regarding actions, even if they are learned in the scriptures.
"Therefore, let the crane be summoned.
When this had been done, the king, seeing that the crane had arrived, said:
"O crane, search the fortress with all speed."
The crane bowed and said:
"O King, this great lake has long been well-scouted as a secure fortress;
however, let a collection of supplies be made on an island in its center. For it is said:"
O King, the accumulation of grain is the best of all forms of accumulation;
for even a jewel placed in the mouth cannot sustain one's life. (Hitopadeśa 3.57)
Furthermore:
"For among all tastes, the salty taste is renowned as the best; without it, a seasoned dish becomes like cow dung. (Hitopadeśa 3.58)
The king said, "Go quickly and let everything be carried out.
Having re-entered, the doorkeeper spoke again:
"Your Majesty, a crow named Meghavarṇa has arrived from Siṃhaladvīpa with his retinue and is standing at the gate."
"And he wishes to see Your Majesty’s feet.
The king said, "A crow is wise and has seen much; therefore, he should be accepted. The ruddy sheldrake replied, "Your Majesty,"
It is true;
however, our adversary is a crow, a land-dweller. How can he, who has been appointed to the side of our enemy, be won over?
And so it has been said:
"The fool who abandons his own side and delights in the factions of others is destroyed by his enemies, like the blue-colored jackal. (Hitopadeśa 3.59)
The king said, "How was that? The minister relates:
Story 7.

In a certain forest, there was a jackal who, while wandering at will near a city, fell into a vat of indigo dye. Unable to get out of it afterwards, he remained there in the morning, presenting himself as if dead.
Then, the owner of the indigo vat, realizing that [the man] was dead, lifted him up from there,
carried him to a distance, and abandoned him.
Therefore he fled.

Having gone into the forest, he looked at himself and saw that he was blue in color, and he thought: "I am now of an excellent complexion; why then should I not achieve my own superiority? Having reflected thus, he summoned the jackals.
He said: "I have been consecrated by the Blessed Forest Deity with her own hand with the essence of all medicinal herbs upon the sovereignty of the forest.
Behold my complexion!
Therefore, from this day forward, let the administration of this forest be carried out according to my command."
And the jackals, beholding him of such distinguished appearance,
prostrated themselves with the eight-limbed salutation and said, "As our lord commands.
In this very manner, his sovereignty over all the forest-dwellers was established.
Then, surrounded by his own kinsmen, he established his superiority. Having obtained tigers, lions, and other such noble attendants,
and feeling ashamed upon seeing the jackals in the assembly, he contemptuously cast all his kinsmen far away.
Then, observing the jackals despondent, a certain old jackal made this vow: "Do not despair;
since we, who know his vital points, have been humiliated by this one ignorant of policy in his own presence, we must act so that he perishes."
Since these tigers and others, deceived by his mere appearance, do not recognize him as a jackal but imagine him to be a king,
act in such a way that he may be fully discerned.
And in this matter, it should be carried out as follows:
I say this: at the time of twilight, you must all simultaneously let out a great roar in his presence.
Then, upon hearing that sound, he too will be compelled by his innate nature to make a sound in return; for—
For whatever nature one possesses, that is eternally difficult to transcend;
if a dog were made a king, would he not still eat his own shoes?
Then, having recognized him by his voice, he was to be killed by the tiger.
When that had been carried out accordingly, this event occurred.
And so it has been said:
One's own enemy knows all of one's vulnerabilities, vital points, and strengths;
dwelling within, he consumes one just as fire burns a dry tree. (Hitopadeśa 3.61)
Therefore I say: "Having abandoned one's own side," and so forth.
The king said: "If this is so, nevertheless let this man who has come from afar be seen first;
then consideration should be made regarding his reception."
Cakra said: "Your Majesty,
the spy has been dispatched and the fortress has been prepared."
Therefore, Śuka should also be brought here and sent away;
however, do so accompanied by a force of warriors, and observe him from a distance. For:
Cāṇakya killed Nanda by employing a sharp assassin;
therefore, one who is endowed with heroism should observe a messenger stationed at a great distance.
Then, having convened an assembly, Śuka and the crow were summoned.
Śuka, with his head slightly raised, sat upon the seat provided and said: "O Hiraṇyagarbha!
The illustrious Citravarṇa, the Great King of Kings, commands you: if you have any need for life or for fortune, [then come]."
"Then come quickly and prostrate at our feet;
otherwise, consider another place to stay.
The king said with anger: "Ah!"
"Is there no one in our assembly who can seize him by the throat?
Then Meghavarna rose and said, "Your Majesty, give the command;
I shall slay this wicked parrot."
The omniscient one, consoling both the king and the crow, said: "My good sir, do not speak thus! Listen for a moment:
that is no assembly where there are no elders."
Those who do not speak the Dharma are not elders;
that which lacks truth is not Dharma for us,
and that which resorts to deceit is not truth.
For this is the duty of kings:
even a barbarian envoy must not be slain, since the king has his envoy as his mouth;
for even when weapons are raised, an envoy speaks nothing other than the truth.
Furthermore:
Who indeed would believe, based on the words of a messenger, that one's own side is inferior and the other's superior?
For a messenger always speaks everything with the assurance that he himself is never to be harmed. (Hitopadeśa 3.65)
Then the king and the crow returned to their natural states.
The parrot also rose and departed;
subsequently, the ruddy goose brought him back, awakened him, gave him golden ornaments and other gifts, and sent him off, whereupon he went to his own country.
The parrot also went to the Vindhya mountain and paid homage to his king, Citravarṇa.
Upon seeing him, the king said: "Parrot!"
"What is the news? What is that country like?
The parrot replied: "Your Majesty, this is the news in brief."
Now, let preparations for war be made;
for how can that land, Karpūradvīpa, be described as being a single portion of heaven, and its king as being like a second Lord of Heaven?
Then the king, having summoned all the learned men, sat down to deliberate and said to them: "Now, regarding the war that must be undertaken, give me instruction on what ought to be done;
for war must certainly be waged."
And so it has been said:
"The twice-born are ruined by discontent, and kings by contentment;
a courtesan is ruined by modesty, and a woman of noble family by shamelessness. (Hitopadeśa 3.66)
The vulture minister named Dūradarśin said: "Your Majesty, war is not the proper course when one is in a state of calamity. For it is said:
'When one's friends, ministers, and circle of well-wishers are firmly devoted...'"
At that time, one should wage war against enemies in such a way as to bring about their downfall.
Furthermore:
Territory, allies, and gold—these three are the fruits of war; when it is certain that these will be obtained, then one should wage war. (Hitopadeśa 3.68)
The king said: "Let the minister first observe my army;
then let it be known how these [weapons] may be employed.
Let an astrologer be summoned in this manner."
Having determined an auspicious moment for the expedition, let him set out. The minister said: "O King, even so, it is improper to undertake an expedition in haste; for: [Verse follows]"
Those fools who rashly enter the enemy's strength without deliberation will certainly receive the embrace of a sword’s edge. (Hitopadeśa 3.69)
The king said: "Minister, do not by any means dampen my enthusiasm;
speak in such a way that one who desires victory may advance upon the territory of his enemy."
The vulture said:
"O King, I shall tell you that;
however, it yields fruit only when it is actually carried out."
And so it has been said:
"What is the use of a king’s knowledge of the scriptures if he does not practice the mantra?
For the alleviation of a disease never occurs merely through a thorough knowledge of the medicine. (Hitopadeśa 3.70)
Since the king’s command is not to be transgressed, I report it exactly as I have heard it; listen, O Lord:
"O King, wherever there is danger—in rivers, mountains, forests, or difficult terrains—there the commander-in-chief shall advance with his forces drawn up in battle array. (Hitopadeśa 3.71)
The commander-in-chief, accompanied by brave men, should march at the front;
in the middle should be the women, the sovereign, the treasury, and whatever force is weak.
On both flanks were horses; beside the horses were chariots;
beside the chariots were elephants; and beside the elephants were foot soldiers.
Afterwards, the king, accompanied by his ministers and brave warriors, should take up the army and advance slowly, comforting those who are weary, with the commander-in-chief leading the way.
The uneven terrain, rich with water and abounding in mountains, should be traversed by elephants;
level ground by horses; and water by boats; while infantry may proceed everywhere. (Hitopadeśa 3.75)
The movement of elephants is declared to be auspicious at the onset of the rainy season;
for other times, however, that of horses and foot-soldiers is always indeed recommended.
In mountainous regions and on difficult paths, the king must provide protection;
even when guarded by his own warriors, he should rest in the sleep of yoga.
One should destroy and weaken enemies by crushing their fortresses and thorns;
and upon entering a foreign land, one should station forest-dwellers at the front.
Where there is a king, there is a treasury; without a treasury, there is no kingship.
Therefore, one should give to brave warriors; for who would not fight on behalf of a giver?
For it is said:
"O King, a man is not the slave of another man; rather, he is the slave of wealth.
Dignity or insignificance depend entirely upon the presence or absence of riches. (Hitopadeśa 3.80)
He should fight without distinction and protect one another;
furthermore, he should place whatever weak troops there may be in the center of the battle formation.
The protector of the earth should station his foot-soldiers in front of the army;
having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and afflict his kingdom.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground. (Hitopadeśa 3.83)
One should constantly spoil his fodder, water, and fuel; likewise, one should break his tanks, as well as his ramparts and moats. (Hitopadeśa 3.84)
O Lord of the Earth, no other elephant among the forces is as preeminent as this one;
for by its own very limbs, it is considered a Mātaṅga endowed with eight weapons.
Since the strength of armies is like a mobile rampart,
a king who possesses superior cavalry will be victorious in a land-based conflict.
And so it has been said:
"Even when fighting while mounted on horses, they are difficult even for the gods to conquer;
yet their enemies, though standing at a distance, have them in the palm of their hand. (Hitopadeśa 3.87)
Leading the first charge in battle, protecting the entire force,
and clearing the paths through the various directions— these are declared to be the duties of the infantry.
They know that an army consisting mostly of well-known kṣatriyas—who are brave by nature, skilled in weapons, undaunted, tireless, and resolute—is the very best. (Hitopadeśa 3.89)
O King, men on earth do not fight for the sake of riches bestowed by many, in the same way that they fight for the honor conferred by their lord. (Hitopadeśa 3.90)
One should prefer a small but solid force rather than a circle of shaven-headed monks;
for the destruction of a worthless force clearly brings about the destruction of even a solid one.
Lack of faith, failure to provide support, seizing one's rightful share, wasting the time [of service], and offering no remedy—these are the causes of disaffection. (Hitopadeśa 3.92)
Desiring victory, one should march against the enemies without afflicting one's own army;
for the enemy host is easily overcome when it is exhausted by long marches. (Hitopadeśa 3.93)
Since there is no other heir who causes such division among his enemies as he does,
one should therefore strive diligently to raise up an heir for that adversary.
An assailant may incite internal rebellion against a steadfast ruler by acting in concert with either the crown prince or the chief minister. (Hitopadeśa 3.95)
One should also destroy a cruel enemy by inflicting a defeat in battle, or else by means of cattle-theft and the subsequent binding of those who rely upon his chief ministers. (Hitopadeśa 3.96)
A king should cause his own kingdom to be inhabited by settling it from foreign lands;
for that kingdom, when settled through gifts and honors, indeed becomes a granter of wealth.
Or rather, what is the use of much speaking?
Self-advancement and the decline of others—this twofold policy is all there is;
by adopting this, the wise attain the status of masters of speech. (Hitopadeśa 3.98)
The king smiled and said: "All this has been stated in detail;
however, one thing is unrestrained nature, while another is that which is governed by scripture.
For how can there be a common substratum between light and darkness? (Hitopadeśa 3.99)

Then the king rose and set out at the auspicious moment announced by the astrologers. Now, a spy who had been dispatched as an emissary approached Hiraṇyagarbha, bowed, and said: "Your Majesty, King Citravarna has almost arrived."
At present, his camp is stationed on the plateau of the Malaya mountain;
the inspection of the fortifications must be carried out at every moment,
for that vulture is a great minister.
Furthermore, through a conversation involving confidential matters with someone, I perceived this hint from him:
that he had already stationed someone within our fortress.
The Cakravāka said: "O King!"
"He must surely be a crow," [the king] said.
"Never! the king replied.
"If that is so, then how was it that he made an effort to overcome the parrot?"
Furthermore, because of Śuka’s arrival, there was an eagerness for war on his part;
moreover, he has been staying here for a long time.
The minister said: "Even so, a newcomer must be regarded with suspicion."
The king said: "Even strangers are sometimes seen to be benefactors. Listen:
A stranger who is beneficial is a kinsman; a kinsman who is harmful is a stranger.
A disease born of one's own body is harmful, while medicine from the forest is beneficial. (Hitopadeśa 3.100)
Furthermore:
There was a servant of King Śūdraka named Vīravara, who in a short time gave up his own son. (Hitopadeśa 3.101)
The Cakravāka asks: "How was that?
The King relates:
Story 8.
Formerly, I was in love with Karpūramañjarī, the daughter of a royal swan named Karpūrakeli, in the pleasure-lake of King Śūdraka.
A prince named Vīravara, having arrived from some distant land, approached the palace gate and said to the doorkeeper: "I am a prince seeking a livelihood; please grant me an audience with the king."
Then he was introduced by him to the king's presence and said, "Your Majesty,
if you have need of me as a servant, then let my livelihood be provided."
Śūdraka said, "What is your livelihood?
Vīravara replied, "Give me five hundred gold pieces every day.
The king asked, "What are your requirements?"
Vīravara said, "I have two arms,
and a sword is the third. The king said, "This is not possible."
Having heard that, Vīravara bowed and set out.
Then the ministers said, "Your Majesty,
let his true nature be ascertained by providing him with provisions for four days."
"Is he using this sustenance for his livelihood, or is he not?
Then, at the minister's word, they summoned him, gave betel to Vīravara, and bestowed five hundred gold pieces upon him;
and the king closely scrutinized the expenditure of that sustenance.
Half of that was given by Vīravara to the gods and the brahmins; half of what remained was given to the suffering;
and the remainder was spent on food and luxuries.
Having performed all these daily duties, he waits at the king’s gate day and night with sword in hand;
and whenever the king himself gives an order, then he even goes to his own home.
Then once, on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that king heard the sound of piteous lamentation.
Having heard it, the king said, "Who is there at the door?
Then he replied, "O King!"
"I am Vīravara.
The king said, "Let him be pursued according to his cries. Vīravara replied, "As Your Majesty commands."
Having said this, he departed.
And the king thought: "It is not fitting that I have sent this prince here all alone into darkness so thick that even a needle could not pierce it."
"Therefore, I too shall go and investigate what this is.
Then the king also took up his sword and went out from the city, following in that man's tracks.
Having gone there, Vīravara saw a certain woman weeping, endowed with beauty and youth, and adorned with every ornament.
And she was asked, "Who are you? Why do you weep?
The woman replied, "I am the royal fortune of this Śūdraka."
"After resting for a long time with great comfort in the shade of his arm,
I shall now go elsewhere. Vīravara said, "Since danger may arise..."
"There is indeed a means for that.
How then might your dwelling here be possible?
Lakṣmī said: 'If you offer your own son Śaktidhara, who is endowed with the thirty-two marks, as a sacrificial gift to the Blessed One Sarvamaṅgalā,'"
"Then I shall dwell here once more for a very long time.
Having said this, she became invisible.
Then Vīravara went to his own home and awakened his sleeping wife and son.
Abandoning their sleep, the two rose and sat down.
Vīravara related all those words of Lakṣmī.
Having heard that, Śaktidhara said joyfully, "I am blessed to be such as this!"
Father, since he is useful for the purpose of protecting the master’s kingdom,
what now is the reason for delay?
The employment of the body in such a task is praiseworthy; for:
"A wise person should renounce both wealth and life itself for the sake of another.
Since destruction is certain, it is better to renounce them for that purpose. (Hitopadeśa 3.102)
Śaktidharamātā said: "If this must not be done, then by what other deed will there be a repayment for the great debt we have incurred?
Having reflected thus, they all went to the abode of Sarvamaṅgalā.
There, having worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā, Vīravara said: "O Goddess!"
Be gracious! May the great king Śūdraka be victorious!
Let this offering be accepted.
Having said this, he cut off his son's head.
Then Vīravara reflected: "I have fulfilled my obligation to the king;
now, enough with life for me who am childless."
Having reflected thus, he cut off his own head;
then the woman also, afflicted by grief for her husband and son, did the same.
Seeing all this, the king thought with wonder:
Beings like me, these lowly creatures, are born and die;
there has never been one like him in this world, nor will there ever be.
"What need have I for this kingdom, now that it has been abandoned? Then Śūdraka also raised his sword to cut off his own head;
thereupon, the Blessed One Sarvamaṅgalā, appearing in person, seized the king by the hand.
And it was said: "Son, I am pleased with you;
enough of such recklessness."
"Even at the end of your life, there shall be no loss of your kingdom.
And the king, having prostrated himself with the eight limbs of his body, said: "O Queen, what use have I for a kingdom?"
"What use have I for life?
If I am worthy of compassion, then let this Vīravara, along with his wife and son, live even by the remainder of my own lifespan;
otherwise, I shall go to whatever destiny awaits me."
The Blessed Lady said: "My son, I am entirely satisfied by this excellence of yours as a being and by your affection for your servant.
Go; may you be victorious."
"May this prince also live, together with his retinue!
Having said this, the goddess vanished.
Then Vīravara, having regained life for himself, his son, and his wife, went to his own home.
The king, too, unobserved by them, quickly entered the inner apartments.
Then at dawn, Vīravara was standing at the gate and, being questioned again by the monarch, he said:
"O Lord, she, weeping, looked at me and vanished from sight."
"No other news whatsoever exists.

Having heard those words, the king was satisfied and thought with wonder: "How is this praiseworthy being of great courage? For it is said: 'One should speak kindly without being fawning; one should be brave without being boastful.'"
A donor should not rain [gifts] upon the unworthy; he should be confident yet not harsh.
"This mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) contains everything within it. Thereupon, the king convened an assembly of learned men in the morning,
recounted the entire account, and out of favor bestowed upon him the kingdom of Karṇāṭaka.
"In that case, is one who is merely a newcomer corrupted simply by birth?
Even among them, there are those who are superior, inferior, and middling.
The ruddy goose replied:
Is he who advises what ought not to be done as if it were right a true minister by the king's will? It is better for the master to suffer mental distress than his destruction through improper action.
That king whose physician, preceptor, and minister speak only pleasant words quickly falls away from his body, his dharma, and his treasury.
Listen, O King:
that which was obtained by one through merit shall also be mine.
For, having killed a monk out of delusion, the barber who sought wealth has been slain.
The king asks: "How was that? The minister relates:
Story 9.
In the city of Ayodhyā, there was a kṣatriya named Cūḍāmaṇi.
Seeking wealth, he propitiated the Blessed One whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon for a long time with great hardship.
Then, his sins exhausted, the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said:
"Commanded by the Lord of Akṣas at the instruction of the Blessed One, you shall today at dawn have yourself shaved;
then, holding a staff in hand, you will stand hidden at the door of your own house. Whichever mendicant you see arrive in the courtyard, you shall strike that clever man with a blow of the staff."
Then, at that very moment, that mendicant became a golden pitcher;
by means of it, you shall live happily for as long as you live.
Thereupon, when he had acted accordingly, that event occurred.
Thereupon, the barber who had been brought there for the purpose of shaving reflected upon seeing all that: "Aha! This is the means to obtain a treasure.
Why then should I not do the same?
From that time forward, that barber, with a club in hand, waited daily in such a manner for the arrival of the mendicant in secret.
Once, a monk who had arrived there was struck with a club by him;
because of that offense, he too was executed by the king's men.
Therefore I say: "That which was obtained by one through merit," and so forth.
The king said:
"How can another person be determined by recounting tales of past events?
Might he be a friend without cause, or perhaps a betrayer of trust? (Hitopadeśa 3.108)
Let it be; let us attend to the matter at hand.
If Citravarna is on the plateau of the Malaya mountains, what should be done now? The minister says: "O King!"
"I have heard from the mouth of Āgatapraṇidhi that because Citravarṇa showed disregard for the instruction of the great minister Gṛdhra, that fool can now be conquered.
And so it has been said:"
Avaricious, cruel, lazy, untruthful, negligent, timid, fickle, foolish, and contemptuous of his warriors—such an enemy is said to be easily destroyed. (Hitopadeśa 3.109)

Therefore, as long as he does not block the gates of our fortress, let the army commanders Sārasa and the others be appointed to destroy his forces in the rivers, mountains, forests, and on the roads.
And so it has been said:
Exhausted by the long journey, beset by rivers, mountains, and forests, terrified by the fear of terrible fires, and likewise afflicted by hunger and thirst. (Hitopadeśa 3.110)
One who is negligent, preoccupied with food, afflicted by disease or famine, unstable, lacking in abundance, and overwhelmed by rain and wind. (Hitopadeśa 3.111)
A ruler of the earth should destroy an enemy army that is thus situated—covered in mud, dust, and water; utterly disordered; and fleeing from bandits. (Hitopadeśa 3.112)
Furthermore:

Out of fear of a sudden attack, a king should always slay his enemy while he is sleeping during the day, exhausted by the fatigue of staying awake and with his soldiers overwhelmed by drowsiness. (Hitopadeśa 3.113)
"Therefore, let our generals go with force against him while he is negligent and strike him day and night as the opportunity arises.
When this was carried out, many of Citravarna's soldiers and generals were slain.
Thereupon, Citravarna became despondent and said to his minister Dūradarśin: "Dear sir!"
Why is this neglect shown toward me? Is there perhaps some lack of decorum on my part?
And so it has been said:
One should not behave improperly simply because one has attained sovereignty; for lack of discipline destroys prosperity, just as old age destroys the most excellent beauty.
Moreover:

The skillful man attains prosperity; he who eats wholesome food enjoys health; the healthy man finds happiness; the industrious man reaches the end of his undertakings; and the disciplined man wins virtue, wealth, and fame. (Hitopadeśa 3.115)
The vulture said: "O King, listen!
Even an unlearned ruler attains supreme prosperity by serving those advanced in knowledge, just as a tree situated near water [thrives]. (Hitopadeśa 3.116)
And furthermore:
"Women, hunting, gambling, and the corruption of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and punishment—these are the vices of kings. (Hitopadeśa 3.117)
Furthermore:
[He is] neither one who follows the flavor of absolute recklessness,
nor one whose inner self is impaired by [wrong] means.
Exalted prosperities can be attained;
for both statesmanship and valor are the abodes of true wealth.
Observing your own strength and enthusiasm, I—
who am solely devoted to daring deeds— paid no heed even to those counsels and spoke with harshness.
Therefore, this fruit of bad policy is being experienced.
And so it has been said:
"To what evil counselor do the faults of policy not resort?"
Whom do diseases not torment when they consume what is unwholesome?
Whom does prosperity not intoxicate? Whom does death not strike down?
And whom do sensual pleasures caused by women not cause to suffer? (Hitopadeśa 3.119)
Furthermore:
sorrow destroys joy, the arrival of winter destroys autumn, the sun destroys darkness, and ingratitude destroys merit.
The birth of a beloved brings grief; improper conduct brings calamity; and even abundant prosperity is destroyed by misconduct.
Then I too reflected: "This king is devoid of wisdom;

otherwise, how could he obscure the moonlight of the discourse on the treatises of political ethics (*nīti-śāstra*) with the torches of his own words? For: What does a scripture do for one who possesses no wisdom of their own?"
What will a mirror do for one who is deprived of eyes? (Hitopadeśa 3.121)
Having reflected thus, I too remained silent.
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, said: "Father, this is my transgression."
"Now, instruct me on how I may return with my remaining forces and go to the Vindhya mountains.
The vulture thought to himself: "A remedy must be devised for this situation; for:"
Anger should always be restrained toward deities, teachers, cows, kings, and Brahmins, as well as toward children, the elderly, and the sick. (Hitopadeśa 3.122)
The minister, smiling, said: "O King, do not fear;
take heart. Listen, O King:
[the skill] of ministers in reconciling broken alliances is like that of physicians in treating a disorder of the humors (sāṃnipātika)."
Wisdom is revealed in action; for who is not wise when things go well?
Furthermore:
The ignorant undertake only small tasks and become distracted; those of firm resolve undertake great undertakings and remain undisturbed. (Hitopadeśa 3.124)
"Therefore, having broken this fortress by your majesty alone, I shall lead you, together with your fame and power, to the Vindhya mountains before long.
The king said, "How can that be accomplished now with such a small force?"
The vulture said: "O King, everything will come to pass;
for lack of procrastination on the part of one who desires victory is an indispensable sign of the attainment of success."
"Therefore, let the blockade of the fortress gates be carried out immediately.
Then Baka, having returned with the dispatched spy, said to Hiraṇyagarbha:
"Your Majesty, this King Citravarṇa, possessing very little strength, will come here supported by the words of the vulture and attempt to blockade the fortress gates."
The royal swan said: "Let an assessment of the strength and weakness within your own forces be made;
having understood that, let gifts of gold, garments, and the like be bestowed as appropriate favors. For it is said:
'He who [recovers] even a single kākīṇī coin fallen upon a pathless road...'"
Even if one were to give away thousands of gold coins at times numbering in the millions with open-handed generosity,
Fortune does not abandon that lion among kings. (Hitopadeśa 3.125)
And furthermore:
"In a sacrifice, at a wedding, in times of calamity, upon the destruction of an enemy, in a deed that brings glory, or in the gathering of friends— "
O lord of men, excessive expenditure does not occur in these eight circumstances: toward beloved women, nor toward impoverished kinsmen.
For it is said:
"A fool indeed brings about total ruin out of fear of a small expenditure;
what wise man would abandon a vessel of white [silver] out of excessive apprehension? (Hitopadeśa 3.127)

The king said, "How is such excessive expenditure appropriate at this time? For it is said: 'One should save wealth for times of calamity. The minister replied, "How can there be calamities for those who possess prosperity?"
The king said, "Sometimes fortune wavers. The minister replied, "Even when accumulated, it perishes;
therefore, O Lord," he continued.
Abandoning all parsimony, let your own warriors be honored with gifts and respect.
As it has been said:
"Knowing one another, filled with joy, and firmly resolved to sacrifice their lives."
Those of noble birth, when properly honored, conquer the forces of their enemies. (Hitopadeśa 3.128)
Furthermore:
"Brave warriors who are endowed with virtue, united, and resolute—even five hundred such heroes can destroy an enemy host. (Hitopadeśa 3.129)
Moreover:
Even by the learned, a man who knows no bounds, who is fierce, who destroys what has been done, and who is self-indulgent—is abandoned; how much more so by others? (Hitopadeśa 3.130)
For it is said:
Truth, valor, compassion, and generosity—these are the great virtues of a king;
a protector of the earth who is abandoned by these indeed incurs reproach. (Hitopadeśa 3.131)
On such an occasion, the ministers must certainly be placed at the forefront.
As it has been said:
"He who is bound to another should rise and fall together with him."
Once he has gained his trust, he should be appointed to oversee both one's life and one's wealth.
For it is said:
"The king whose ministers are a rogue, a woman, or a child sinks into the ocean of improper conduct, tossed about by the winds of bad policy. (Hitopadeśa 3.133)
Listen, O King:

"He whose joy and anger are restrained, who has conviction in the meaning of the scriptures, and who constantly looks after his servants—for him the earth shall be a giver of wealth. (Hitopadeśa 3.134)
A king should never despise those ministers with whom his own rise and fall are inevitably linked. (Hitopadeśa 3.135)
For when a king, blinded by pride, stumbles like an elephant in rut that has lost its sense of direction,
it is only the well-instructed who are called upon to provide him with a supporting hand.
Then Meghavarṇa, having arrived and bowed, said: "O King, grant me the favor of your glance;
the enemy is now stationed at the gate of the fortress."
"Therefore, by the command of Your Majesty's feet, I shall go outside and display my own prowess;
through that, I shall discharge my debt to Your Majesty's feet.
The ruddy goose replied, "Do not do so!"
If one must go out to fight, then taking refuge in a fortress is indeed useless. Furthermore:
"Just as even a formidable crocodile falls under control when it emerges from the water,"
Even a brave lion, once it has emerged from the forest, may become like a jackal.
Then they all went to the gate of the fortress and engaged in a great battle.
On the following day, King Citravarna said to the vulture, "Father,
fulfill now that which you have promised."
The crow said:
"O King, go yourself and witness the battle;
for a king should lead his forces into combat while keeping a watchful eye."
Does not even a dog certainly act like a lion when presided over by its master? (Hitopadeśa 3.138)

The vulture said: "O King, listen for a moment— A fortress that cannot endure adversity, is extremely small, has a foolish and addicted leader, and lacks protection from cowardly soldiers, is said to be in a state of calamity. (Hitopadeśa 3.139)
Therefore, that [set of four] is not present here:
"Sowing dissension, a long siege, a sudden assault, and fierce valor—these are said to be the four means for storming a fort. (Hitopadeśa 3.140)
Here, an effort is made according to one's ability;
he whispers into his ear, "It is even so, even so.
Then, before the sun had even risen, battle broke out at all four gates of the fortress.
Once, fire was cast into the houses within the fortress by crows.

Then, hearing the clamor, "The fortress has been seized! It has been seized! and seeing the fire blazing on all sides, many royal swan soldiers and the fortress inhabitants quickly entered the lake; for it is said:
One should act according to one's ability at the time of action—whether it be well-counseled, a bold advance, a good fight, or a strategic retreat—but one should not hesitate. (Hitopadeśa 3.141)
King Haṃsa, being by nature slow of gait, was accompanied by Sārasa;
he was approached and surrounded by Kukkuṭa, the commander-in-chief of Citravarṇa.
Hiraṇyagarbha said to Sārasa: "Commander-in-chief!"
"O crane, why do you destroy yourself out of consideration for me?
At present, I am unable to go."
"You are still capable of going;
therefore, go and enter the water to protect yourself.
With the consent of the Omniscient One, you shall make our son, named Cūḍāmaṇi, the king."
The crane said: "O King, such unbearable words must not be spoken;
as long as the moon and sun remain in the sky, may Your Majesty be victorious!"
"O King, I am the superintendent of the fortress.
Therefore, let the enemy enter by a path whose gateways are smeared with my flesh and blood.
Furthermore, O King—"
"A master who is generous, patient, and appreciative of merit is difficult to find.
The King said, "That is indeed true; however, I know that even a servant who is pure, capable, and loyal is hard to obtain. (Hitopadeśa 3.142)
The crane said: "Listen, O King!
If there is no fear of death by abandoning the battle, then it is proper to depart from here to another place."
Now, since death is inevitable for every living being, why is one's reputation needlessly sullied? // Hit_3.143 //
And furthermore:
In this existence, which is as fragile as the flickering of waves tossed by the wind, the sacrifice of one’s life for the sake of others arises through the power of merit. (Hitopadeśa 3.144)

The sovereign, the minister, the realm, the fortification, the treasury, the army, and the ally—these are the constituent parts of a kingdom; as are the subjects and the guilds of the citizens. (Hitopadeśa 3.145)
"Your Majesty, you are our master and must be protected by all means. For:
'Even if she is prosperous, a wife who abandons her husband does not survive;
what can even the physician Dhanvantari do for one whose life has departed? (Hitopadeśa 3.146)
Furthermore:
When the lord of men closes his eyes, this world of living beings closes its own;
and when he rises, it rises, just as the lotus does at the rising of the sun. (Hitopadeśa 3.147)
In this matter as well, the king is the primary limb.
Then, a cock arrived and struck the body of the royal swan with its very sharp claws.
Thereupon, the crane quickly approached, shielded the king with his own body, and cast him into the water.
Then, although the crane was shattered by the blow of the cock's claw, he struck down many of the cock's army;
subsequently, the crane himself was encountered by many birds, who tore him apart with beak-strikes and killed him. Then Citravarṇa entered the fortress.
Having caused the goods situated in that difficult place to be seized, and gladdened by the bards with shouts of victory, he went to his own military camp.
Then the princes said: "Among those royal swans, that crane alone was meritorious, by whom the lord was protected through the sacrifice of his own body. For:"
All cows produce offspring that possess the form of cattle;
yet only a rare one gives birth to the Lord of Cattle, whose shoulders are marked by the scratches of horns.
Viṣṇuśarman said: "Let that great being, surrounded by Vidyādharīs, enjoy for as long as he desires those imperishable worlds purchased with his courage.
And so it has been said:
'And those heroes who, for the sake of their master, have surrendered their lives in battles...'"
Those men who are devoted to their masters and grateful go to heaven.
Wherever a hero is slain while surrounded by enemies,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not succumb to cowardice.
Then Viṣṇuśarman said, "The 'War' has been heard by you.
The princes replied, "Having heard it, we have become happy.
Viṣṇuśarman said, "Let another [book] be likewise."
May there never be for you, O rulers of the earth, any conflict involving elephants, horses, or infantry,
as you are struck down by the winds of political wisdom and counsel.
Let the enemies take refuge in mountain caves.
Thus ends the third collection of stories, titled "War," in the *Hitopadeśa*, a treatise on ethics composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita.
