Furthermore, at the commencement of the discourse, the princes said: "Noble sir,
we have heard of war."
"Let the peace treaty now be declared.
Viṣṇuśarman said, "Listen;
I shall also describe the treaty."
Of which this is the first verse:
"When a great battle had occurred between two kings whose armies were slain, peace was established in an instant by the speech of two steady vultures. (Hitopadeśa 4.1)
The princes asked, "How was that?
Viṣṇuśarman relates: Then that royal swan said, "By whom was fire cast into our fortress? Is it by an enemy?"

"Or could it be someone living in our fortress who has been employed by the enemy? The ruddy goose replied, "Your Majesty, that Meghavarṇa, along with his retinue, is not to be seen; he is your friend without cause."
"Therefore, I believe this is his very own doing.
Having reflected for a moment, the king said, "It may well be so;
this is my own ill fortune."
And so it has been said:
"This is the fault of fate, and not of the ministers;
a well-executed task may perish somewhere due to the conjunction of fate. (Hitopadeśa 4.2)
Having encountered adverse circumstances, an unwise man blames fate;
he does not recognize the faults of his own actions. (Hitopadeśa 4.3)
Furthermore:
He who does not welcome the words of friends who desire his welfare, that person of evil intellect perishes like the turtle who fell from the wood. (Hitopadeśa 4.4)
Furthermore:
Speech must always be guarded, for from speech comes destruction, just as in the case of the tortoise being carried away by two geese who caused him to fall. (Hitopadeśa 4.5)
The king asked, "How was that?
The minister related:
Story 1.
In the land of Magadha there is a lake named Phullotpala;
there two geese named Saṅkaṭa and Vikaṭa lived for a long time,
and a tortoise named Kambugrīva dwelt there as their friend.
Then one day, some fishermen arrived and spoke thus: "Having stayed here today, we must kill the fish, tortoises, and other creatures tomorrow morning.
Upon hearing this, the tortoise said to the two swans, "Friends, I have overheard this conversation of the fishermen."
"Now, what should I do?
The two swans replied, "Let it be known for now;
tomorrow morning, whatever is appropriate shall be done."
The tortoise said: "Do not speak thus;
for I have personally witnessed what transpired here, as it has been said:"
The one who provides for the future and the one with presence of mind—these two alone thrive in happiness; whereas the one who merely speculates on what will be perishes.
The two of them asked, "How was that?
The tortoise relates:
Story 2.
Formerly, when fishermen of this very kind had arrived at this very lake, three fish deliberated among themselves.
Among them was one fish named Anāgatavidhātā (Foreseer).
He said: "I shall go to another body of water for now."
Having said this, he went to another lake. Another fish, named Pratyutpannamati, said: "Since there is no means of knowing the future, where should I go?
When the situation arises, I shall act as required."
And so it has been said:
"He who overcomes a calamity that has arisen is wise, just as the lover was concealed from view by the merchant’s wife. (Hitopadeśa 4.7)
Yadbhaviṣya asks: "How was that?
Pratyutpannamati relates:
Story 3.
Formerly, in Vikramapura, there was a merchant named Samudradatta.
His wife, named Ratnaprabhā, constantly took pleasure with her own servant. For it is said:
"To women, no one is particularly disliked, nor is anyone particularly dear."
Like cattle in a forest seeking fresh grass, they desire ever-new [objects]. (Hitopadeśa 4.8)

Then one day, as Ratnaprabhā was giving a kiss upon the face of that servant, she was observed by Samudradatta. Thereupon, that unchaste woman quickly went to her husband and said, "My lord, this servant has committed a great offense."
"Since he has committed this theft and is eating camphor, I have known it by smelling his mouth. And so it is said:
The food of women is said to be twofold, their intelligence fourfold,
their resolve sixfold, and their desires eightfold.
Hearing this, the servant also spoke with anger: "My Lord,
how can a servant remain in the house of a master who has such a wife,
where every moment the mistress sniffs at the face of the servant?"
Then he rose up and started to move;
the good man, having awakened him with effort, restrained him.
Therefore I say: "When misfortune has arisen," and so forth.

Then, that which was said by Yadbhaviṣya: "What is not to be will not be; and what is to be will not be otherwise"—why is this medicine, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk? (Hitopadeśa 4.10)
Then, in the morning, Pratyutpannamati was caught in the net; he remained there, making himself appear as if dead.
Once he was pulled out of the net, he leaped with all his might and entered deep water. Yadbhaviṣya, however, was captured by the fishermen and killed.
Therefore I say: "Providing for the future," and so forth.
"Please act in such a way that I may reach another lake.
The two swans replied, "Once you have reached another body of water, all will be well with you."
"What is the procedure for you when traveling on land?
The tortoise said, "Let it be arranged so that I may travel with you through the path of the sky."
The two swans said, "How is such a means possible?
The tortoise replied, "A single piece of wood must be held in your beaks, and I shall support it with my mouth;
then, by the strength of your wings, I too shall travel with ease."
The two swans said: "This means is possible;
however, a wise man should consider both the means and the potential failure.
While the foolish crane looked on, his sons were devoured by mongooses. (Hitopadeśa 4.11)
The tortoise asks: "How was that?
The two of them relate:
Story 4.
In the northern region, on a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa, there is a great Pippala tree.
Many cranes dwell there.
Beneath that tree, in a hollow, a snake resides.
He was devouring the young offspring of the cranes.
Then, hearing the lamentation of those afflicted by grief, a certain old crane said: "O friends, do this:
taking fish, scatter them one by one in a line starting from the hole of the mongoose and extending as far as the hole of the snake."
Then, mongooses, greedy for that food, will come and see the snake; out of natural enmity, they must kill it. When this has been carried out, that purpose will be accomplished.
Then, the cries of the young cranes atop the tree were heard by the mongooses;
subsequently, having climbed that tree, the young cranes were eaten.
Therefore, we say: "While devising a stratagem," and so forth.
Seeing you being led away by us, people will surely say something;
if you give an answer, then it will be your death.
"Therefore, you must remain exactly as you are.
The tortoise said, "Am I unwise? I will not give an answer."
"I must not say anything.
When this was carried out, and having seen such a tortoise, all the cowherds ran after it and said, "Aha!"
It is a great marvel!
A tortoise is being carried away by two birds.
Someone says: "If this tortoise falls,"
Then, some said, "It should be cooked and eaten right here";
another said, "It should be roasted on the bank of the lake and eaten"; and yet another said, "It should be taken home and consumed."
Hearing those words, the tortoise, overcome with anger and forgetting his former good conduct, said, "You shall eat ashes! As he spoke, he fell down and was killed by them.
Therefore I say: "Of friends who desire one's welfare," and so forth.
Then the crane *Praṇidhi* arrived there and said, "O King!"
Indeed, I have stated previously that the purification of one's own faults must be performed at every moment;
yet you did not do so, and this is the fruit you now experience for that lack of heedfulness.
The burning of Durgā was carried out by the crow Meghavarṇa, who had been answered by the vulture.
Sighing, the king said:
"He who places his trust in enemies, whether out of affection or because of past favors..."
Like one who has fallen from the top of a tree while asleep, he awakens.

Then Praṇidhi said: "After I have arranged for the burning of this fortress, when Meghavarṇa comes from there, Citravarṇa, being pleased, will say: 'Let this Meghavarṇa be consecrated here in the kingdom of Karpūradvīpa.
And so it was said:"
One should never let the service of a servant who has fulfilled his duty go to waste;
rather, one should gladden him with rewards, with thought, with speech, and with a look. (Hitopadeśa 4.13)
The cakravāka bird said: "Your Majesty, have you heard what Praṇidhi says? The king asked: "And then? And then?"
Praṇidhi said: Then the vulture, the prime minister, spoke: "O King, this is not appropriate.
Let some other favor be granted; for—”
To offer arguments to one who does not investigate is like threshing chaff;
O King, a favor done for the base is like urinating on sand. (Hitopadeśa 4.14)
A base person should never occupy the station of the great.
As it has been said:
"Having attained a praiseworthy position, a base person desires to kill his master."
Just as the mouse, having attained the state of a tiger, went to kill the sage.
Citravarṇa asks: "How was that?
The minister relates:
Story 5.
In the penance grove of the great seer Gautama, there was a sage named Mahātapa.
There, in the vicinity of his hermitage, he saw a young mouse that had fallen from the beak of a crow.
Then, filled with compassion, that sage raised it on grains of wild rice (nīvāra).
Then the cat rushed toward that mouse to devour it;
seeing him, the mouse entered the lap of the sage.
Thereupon, the sage said: "Mouse!"
"May you become a cat.
Thereupon, that cat, seeing the dog, fled.
Then the sage said, "Are you afraid of the dog?"
"You yourself become a dog. That dog was afraid of the tiger; therefore, the sage turned the dog into a tiger.
Then the sage looked upon that tiger and saw, "This is a mouse."
Then, seeing both that sage and the tiger, everyone said, "By this sage, a mouse has been brought to the state of a tiger.

Hearing this, the tiger, filled with distress, reflected: "As long as this sage remains, this report of my true nature—which brings me ill repute—will not cease; therefore, I shall not flee. Having thus deliberated, the mouse went to kill that sage.
Then the Sage, having understood that, said, "Become a mouse once again," and he was turned back into a mouse. Therefore I say: "A base person, having attained a position of honor," and so forth.
Furthermore, O King:
One should not think, "This is easy. Listen:
Having devoured many fish—superior, inferior, and middling—the crane later died from seizing a crab due to excessive greed. (Hitopadeśa 4.16)
Citravarṇa asks: "How was that?
The minister relates:
Story 6.
In the region of Mālava there is a lake named Padmagarbha.
There, an old crane, devoid of strength, remained standing as if displaying his own distress.
He was seen from afar by a certain crab.
And being asked, "Why do you remain here having abandoned food?", the crane said: "Fish are the cause of my livelihood;
I have heard news at the edge of the city that fishermen will come and kill them."

"Therefore, knowing that death has arrived for us precisely because there is no longer any movement [of the water], we have shown disregard even for food. Then the fish reflected: "At this time, he appears to be truly our benefactor;
therefore, let him be asked what ought to be done."
And so it has been said:
"One should form an alliance with an enemy who is a benefactor, not with a friend who is a wrongdoer;
for benefit and harm are the defining characteristics of these two. (Hitopadeśa 4.17)
The fish said, "O crane, what means of protection is there for us here?
The crane replied, "There is a means of protection: taking refuge in another body of water."
"There I shall lead you to you one by one.
The fish said, "So be it.
Thereupon, that wicked crane led those fish away one by one and ate them.
Immediately thereafter, the crab said to him, "O crane,
take me there as well.
Then the crane, desiring the unprecedented meat of the crab, respectfully led him away and placed him on dry land.
The crab, too, seeing that ground strewn with the bones and thorns of fish, thought: "Alas, I am ruined, unfortunate as I am!
Very well, now I shall act according to the occasion. For:
One should fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived."
But seeing that danger has arrived, let him strike fearlessly. (Hitopadeśa 4.18)
Furthermore:
When a wise man, being attacked and fighting, sees no way out for himself, he dies together with his enemy. (Hitopadeśa 4.19)
Having reflected thus, that crab cut off the neck of the crane;
then the crane met his death.
Therefore I say: "Having devoured many fish," and so forth.
Then Citravarṇa said: "Listen first, O minister; this is what I have reflected upon:
while staying here, this King Meghavarṇa must bring to us as many of the finest goods of Karpūra-dvīpa as there are."
"Therefore, we must remain on the Vindhya mountain with great happiness. Dūradarśin laughed and said: "O King, he who rejoices after having entertained anxieties concerning the future—"
He incurs contempt, like a twice-born man whose vessel has been broken. (Hitopadeśa 4.20)
The king asked, "How was that? The minister related: Story 7.

In a city named Devīkoṭa, there was a Brahmin named Devaśarman. On the occasion of the Mahāviṣuvat saṅkrānti, he obtained a single bowl filled with barley meal. Taking it with him, he fell asleep in a corner of a potter’s warehouse full of vessels, overwhelmed by the heat of the fierce sun.

Then, taking a staff in his hand for the purpose of guarding the barley meal, he thought: "Today, by selling this bowl of barley meal, I shall obtain ten cowrie shells; then, right here, using those cowries, I will purchase a water-jar, a bowl, and so forth. As that wealth increases manifold, I will repeatedly purchase goods such as cloth with that money, and by selling them, I shall turn it into wealth amounting to hundreds of thousands."
I shall perform four marriages;
thereafter, among those wives of mine, I shall feel excessive passion for whichever one possesses beauty and youth.
When my co-wives engage in conflict, [I shall act accordingly].
Then, saying, "Agitated with anger, I shall strike them all with a club," he threw the club;
by it, a bowl of roasted flour was pulverized and many vessels were broken.
Then, when the potter arrived at that sound and saw such vessels, he insulted the Brahmin and cast him out from the pavilion.
Therefore I say: "One should not harbor thoughts of the future," and so forth.
Then the king spoke to the vulture in private: "Father, instruct me on what ought to be done. The vulture replied:
Indeed, the leaders of a king who is arrogant with pride and has gone astray like an elephant in rut come to be censured. (Hitopadeśa 4.21)
"Listen, O King! Was this fortress broken down by us through the pride of our strength, or by a stratagem presided over by your majesty?
The king replied, "By your stratagem."
The vulture said: "If my words are followed, then you should go to your own country;
otherwise, when the rainy season arrives and there is a conflict with an equal force, it will be difficult for us, stationed in enemy territory, even to return to our own land."
Therefore, let us proceed with the aim of securing that happiness and glory;
the fortress has been broken,
and fame has been won as it were.
This is indeed my considered view; for:
"He who, placing righteousness foremost and setting aside both the likes and dislikes of his master, speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial—by him the king has a true companion. (Hitopadeśa 4.22)
Moreover:
"What wise man indeed would place his friends, his army, his kingdom, himself, and even his fame upon the swing of uncertainty in battle? (Hitopadeśa 4.23)
Furthermore:
One should desire peace even with an equal, for victory in battle is uncertain;
"One should not engage in what is doubtful," so said Bṛhaspati. (Hitopadeśa 4.24)
Moreover—In battle, destruction sometimes occurs for both sides;
did not Sundas and Upasundas, though equal in strength, destroy one another? (Hitopadeśa 4.25)
The king said, "How was that? The minister relates:
Story 8.

In ancient times, two brothers of the Daitya race named Sunda and Upasunda, desiring the sovereignty of the three worlds, propitiated the Moon-crested Lord for a long time through great physical austerity.
Then the Blessed One, being well-pleased with them, said, "Choose a boon.

Immediately thereafter, by the power of Sarasvatī who was presiding over their throats, the two, wishing to say one thing, uttered something else: "If you are pleased with us, then [give us] your own beloved..."
May the Supreme Lord grant Pārvatī.
Now, because the granting of the boon was unavoidable by the enraged Blessed One,
Pārvatī was given to those two who were bewildered by their deliberations.
Then, by those two who were greedy for her beauty and charm,
who were destroyers of the world, who were eager for slaughter, and who were the darkness of sin—

While they were quarreling with one another, saying "It is mine," and had resolved that some authoritative person should be consulted, that very venerable lord appeared there in the form of an elderly brahmin.
Immediately thereafter, they asked the brahmin, "This [woman] has been obtained by us through our own power; to whom does she belong?
The brahmin replied:

A twice-born man is worthy of honor by virtue of his superior knowledge; a Kṣatriya, even if powerful, is honored for his strength; a Vaiśya is distinguished by his abundance of wealth and grain; but a Śūdra is honored through his service to the twice-born.
When it was said, "Therefore, you two are followers of the kṣatriya dharma;
for you both, the rule is indeed battle," they thought, "He has spoken well," and being equal in prowess,
they met their destruction at the same time by slaying one another.
Therefore I say: "One should desire peace even with an equal," and so forth.
The King said: "Why was this not taught by you earlier? The Minister replied: "At that time, did you hear my words all the way to their conclusion?"
Even then, this undertaking of conflict was not with my consent;
for this Hiraṇyagarbha is endowed with the virtues of a saintly person and should not be opposed.
And so it has been said:

One who is truthful, one whose purpose is righteous, one who is non-Aryan, one who possesses a united brotherhood, one who is powerful, and one who is victorious in many battles—these seven are proclaimed as those with whom peace should be made. (Hitopadeśa 4.27)
Guarding his truth, the noble man does not undergo a change of heart even when bound by it; even at the cost of his life, he clearly does not turn toward unrighteousness. (Hitopadeśa 4.28)
For when a righteous king is attacked, everyone indeed fights for him;
because of his affection for his subjects and his righteousness, a righteous king is difficult to overcome even with great effort.
Even with an ignoble person, a reconciliation should be made when destruction is imminent;
however, without relying upon that [reconciliation], a noble person should not allow time to pass by.
Just as a bamboo thicket surrounded by dense thorns cannot be uprooted, so too it is impossible to destroy one who possesses a multitude of brothers. (Hitopadeśa 4.31)
There is no precedent for one to fight with a stronger opponent; for a cloud never moves against the wind. (Hitopadeśa 4.32)
Like that of Jamadagni’s son, the prowess of one who has been victorious in many battles is broken by everyone, everywhere, and at all times. (Hitopadeśa 4.33)
When one who has been victorious in many battles enters into an alliance, his enemies quickly come under his control through his majesty. (Hitopadeśa 4.34)
"In that case, this king, endowed with many virtues, should be allied with.
The Cakravāka said,
"O spy, everything has been understood."
"Go; you shall return again. Then King Hiraṇyagarbha asked the cakravāka bird, "Minister," he said.
"How many are those who cannot be reconciled?
I wish to hear them.
The minister replied, "O King!"

I shall speak; listen: the child, the old man, the one long afflicted by disease, likewise the one cast out by his kinsmen; the coward, the cowardly person, the greedy, and likewise the greedy person. (Hitopadeśa 4.35)
One whose nature is dispassionate yet excessively attached to sense objects, who possesses a distracted mind regarding mantras, and who reviles the gods and Brahmins; (4.36)
One who is struck by fate, as well as one who is devoted to fate;
one afflicted by the calamity of famine, and one overwhelmed by the calamity of military force. (Hitopadeśa 4.37)

One who stays in an improper place, one with many enemies, one who is not joined with the right time, and one who is devoid of truth and righteousness—these twenty persons [are ruined]. (Hitopadeśa 4.38)
One should not make peace with these, but should instead wage war against them alone;
for when they are attacked, they quickly fall under the power of the enemy. (Hitopadeśa 4.39)
Because a fool possesses little power, the world does not wish to fight him;
for a simpleton is incapable of discerning the fruit of victory or defeat in battle.
Due to a lack of energy and strength, both an old man and one who is long ill are undoubtedly overcome even by their own kin. (Hitopadeśa 4.41)
For one who has been cast out by all his kinsmen becomes easy to destroy;
yet those very kinsmen, having made him their own, are the ones who strike him down. (Hitopadeśa 4.42)
A coward perishes by himself through the abandonment of battle;
likewise, a timid man is abandoned by them in the midst of combat. (Hitopadeśa 4.43)
Because a greedy person does not share his wealth, his dependents will not fight for him;
a king who relies on greedy dependents is destroyed by those very same people when they have been alienated by his lack of generosity.
One whose subjects have become alienated can be subdued by his own people in battle; he becomes as easy to attack as a man who is excessively attached to sensual pleasures. (Hitopadeśa 4.45)
But one whose mind is set on many mantras becomes detestable to practitioners; because his mind is unstable, he is disregarded in the performance of rites. (Hit 4.46)
O Lord, because unrighteousness is always more powerful, one who reviles Brahmins is himself destroyed, being likewise struck down by fate. (Hitopadeśa 4.47)
"Destiny alone is indeed the cause of both prosperity and adversity";
thus, one who is devoted to destiny, reflecting in this way, does not exert himself by his own effort. (Hitopadeśa 4.48)
Afflicted by famine, he himself falls into despair;
for one who is obsessed with the calamity of his army, the power to fight does not arise. (Hitopadeśa 4.49)
For one who stands in an improper place is slain even by a very minor enemy;
even a tiny crocodile drags down even the lord of the waters in the sea. (Hitopadeśa 4.50)
But one who has many enemies is terrified like a pigeon in the midst of hawks;
by whichever path he goes, by that very path he quickly comes to ruin. (Hitopadeśa 4.51)
But an army engaged at the wrong time is destroyed by one who fights at the right time, like a crow whose vision is blinded by an owl at midnight. (Hitopadeśa 4.52)
One should never form an alliance with one who is devoid of truth and righteousness;
for even if such a person is allied, they soon undergo a change of heart due to their inherent wickedness.
I shall further explain: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, and duplicity constitute the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
The means for undertaking actions, and the excellence of personnel and material resources.
The fivefold counsel consists of: the division of place and time,
the remedy for calamities,
and the accomplishment of the task.
The four expedients are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force;
as well as the power of energy and the power of counsel.
The power of the lord and [the power of counsel] constitute the triad of powers.
Having constantly reflected upon all this, the great become desirous of victory;
for that which cannot be obtained even at the cost of sacrificing one's life—
Behold, that Fortune, though fickle, runs even toward one who knows the way of policy.
And as it has been said:
"He whose wealth is always distributed evenly, whose movement is secret, and whose counsel is well-guarded;..."
He who does not speak unpleasantly to living beings rules the earth as far as the edge of the ocean.
But, Your Majesty, although peace has been proposed by the great minister Gṛdhra, it should not yet be accepted by the king out of pride in his victory over the spirits.
Your Majesty!
Therefore, let it be done thus:
let our friend Mahābala, the crane king of Siṃhaladvīpa, incite a rebellion in Jambudvīpa. For—having established a secure defense, with a well-united force—
A hero, moving about with power, should cause his enemy to suffer so that, being equally tormented,
he seeks reconciliation with the one who has tormented him. (Hitopadeśa 4.56)
The king, saying "So be it," dispatched the crane named Vicitra to the island of Siṃhala with a well-concealed letter. Then the spy returned and said, "O King,
please hear first the report concerning that place."
Thus the vulture spoke there: "Your Majesty, Meghavarṇa has lived there for a long time;
he knows whether King Hiraṇyagarbha possesses the qualities of one with whom it is fitting to form an alliance, or not."
Then Meghavarṇa was summoned and questioned by King Citravarṇa:
"Crow, what is King Hiraṇyagarbha like? And what is his minister, the cakravāka, like?"
The crow said: "O Lord, that King Hiraṇyagarbha is equal to Yudhiṣṭhira in his great magnanimity and truthfulness of speech;
a minister equal to the Cakravāka is not to be seen anywhere."
The king said, "If this is so, then how was he deceived by you?
Laughing, Meghavarṇa replied, "Your Majesty,
what skill is there in deceiving those who have placed their trust in one?"
For what indeed can be called manliness in killing one who has fallen asleep while resting on one's lap?
Listen, O King: at our very first meeting, that minister recognized me for who I am;
however, as he is a noble-minded king, I deceived him.
And so it has been said:
"He who, by comparison with himself, understands a wicked man to be a speaker of truth, is deceived by rogues just as the Brahmins were by the goat. (Hitopadeśa 4.58)
The king said: "How was that? Meghavarṇa relates:
Story 9.
There was a certain Brahmin in Gautama’s forest who had prepared a sacrifice;
for the sake of that sacrifice, he had purchased a goat from another village and was carrying it on his shoulder.
"Go; you have been observed by three rogues.
Then those rogues deliberated: "If this goat can be obtained by some means or other, then there will be a preeminent display of wit."
At the foot of three trees, at an interval of one *krośa*, they stood by the path awaiting the arrival of that brahmin.
There, a certain rogue said to the brahmin as he was passing: "O brahmin, why are you carrying a dog on your shoulder?"
The Brahmin said, "This is not a dog,
but a sacrificial goat.
Then, another rogue standing nearby spoke exactly the same thing.
Having heard this, the Brahmin set the goat down on the ground and, after looking at it repeatedly, placed it back upon his shoulder and set off with a wavering mind. For:
"It is true that even the intellect of the virtuous wavers due to the words of the wicked."
And once he has been made to trust by them, he perishes like Citrakarṇa. (Hitopadeśa 4.59)
The king asked, "How was that? He related the story— Story 10.
In a certain forest region, there lived a lion named Madotkaṭa.
He had three servants: a crow, a tiger, and a jackal.
Now, while they were wandering about, they saw a certain camel who had strayed from his caravan.
And when asked, "From where have you come? Why were you separated from your caravan? he related his own story.
Then they took him and delivered him to the lion.
Having granted him the word of safety,
he established him there, giving him the name Citrakarṇa.
Then, at one time, because the lion was afflicted by physical infirmity and due to heavy rains, they were unable to obtain food and became distressed.
Then they deliberated:
"Let it be carried out in such a way that the master kills Citrakarṇa himself;
what use have we for this Kaṇṭakabhuja?"
The tiger said, "This one has been favored by his master being granted a promise of safety;
how, then, can such a thing be possible?
The crow replied, "At a time like this, a master who has fallen into ruin will do even what is wicked. For it is said:"
A woman tormented by hunger might abandon her own son;
a female serpent tormented by hunger might devour its own eggs.
What sin will a hungry person not commit?
Men who are impoverished become devoid of compassion.
And furthermore:
"One who is intoxicated, negligent, insane, exhausted, angry, hungry, greedy, timid, in haste, or lustful does not know the Dharma. (Hitopadeśa 4.61)
Having reflected thus, they all went into the presence of the lion.
The lion asked, "Have you obtained anything for the sake of food?
They replied, "O King!"
"Has anything been obtained even with effort?
The lion asked, "What means of livelihood is there now?
The crow replied, "O King!"
"Is this total destruction brought about by the abandonment of food that is within our own control?
The lion asked, "What food here is within our control?
The crow whispered in his ear, "Citrakarṇa."
The lion touched the ground and touched his ears;
he said, "Having granted him the word of safety, he has been taken in by us.
How then could such a thing be possible? For instance:"
Neither the gift of land, nor the gift of gold,
nor the gift of cattle, nor likewise the gift of food is considered here to be a great gift in the way that they describe it.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of fearlessness is supreme.
And furthermore:
"Whatever fruit belongs to the Aśvamedha sacrifice, which fulfills all desires, that same fruit one obtains by properly protecting one who has come for refuge. (Hitopadeśa 4.63)
The crow said, "He must not be killed by our master;
rather, we ourselves must act in such a way that he agrees to offer up his own body."

Having heard that, the lion remained silent. Then, having found his opportunity, the jackal devised a ruse and, taking them all with him, went into the presence of the lion. Thereupon, the crow said: "O King!"
Despite his efforts, no food was obtained; moreover, my master is distressed by many days of fasting. Therefore, let him now consume my flesh; for:
Indeed, all subjects have their root in the sovereign;
for even when trees possess roots, human effort toward them is fruitful.
The lion said, "My good friend, it is better to give up one's life than to engage in such an action."
The jackal also spoke likewise.
Then the lion said, "Do not do so.
Thereupon the tiger said, "May my lord live by means of my body."
The lion said, "Never is such a thing appropriate.
Then Citrakarṇa, having gained confidence, likewise offered the gift of his own body. Consequently, at those words, that tiger tore open his belly and killed him;
and he was devoured by all of them.
Therefore I say: "The mind wavers; this is the truth," and so forth.
Then, having heard the words of the third rogue and having ascertained the delusion of his own mind, he abandoned the goat.
The Brahmin, having bathed, went home;
and the goat was led away and eaten by those rogues.
Therefore I say: "He who knows by comparison with himself," and so forth.
The king said: "Meghavarṇa, how did you dwell for so long in the midst of enemies?
Or how was conciliation toward them practiced by you?"

Meghavarṇa said: "O Lord, for the sake of one's master's business or by the power of one's own purpose, what is there that is not done? Behold—O King, does the world not carry fuel upon its head in order to burn it?"
Even as they wash the roots of trees, the river's current cuts them away.
And so it has been said:
"A wise man, when faced with a task, may even carry his enemies on his shoulder;
just as the frogs were destroyed by the old serpent. (Hitopadeśa 4.66)
The king asked, "How was that? Meghavarṇa related:
Story 11.
In an old garden there was a snake named Mandaviṣa (Slow-Poison). Because he was extremely decrepit, he was unable even to seek out his own food and remained fallen upon the bank of a lake.
Then, from a distance, he was spotted by a certain frog.
And when asked, "Why does he not seek food for you?
the serpent replied, "Go, good sir;
what is the use of your asking about the circumstances of one as ill-fated as I?"
Then, curiosity having arisen in him, that frog said, "Tell me everything.
The serpent replied, "My good friend,
the son of a Vedic scholar named Kauṇḍinya, a resident of this city, about twenty years of age and endowed with every virtue, was bitten by me, a cruel creature, due to ill fortune."
Then, beholding his son named Suśīla dead,
Kauṇḍinya fainted from grief and rolled upon the ground.
Immediately thereafter, all the kinsmen residing in Brahmapura arrived and sat down there.
And so it has been said:
"He who stands by one in times of festival, in calamity, in battle, in famine, during the upheaval of a kingdom, at the royal gate, and in the cremation ground—he is a kinsman. (Hitopadeśa 4.67)
Thereupon, a bath-graduate named Kapila said: "O Kauṇḍinya, you are a fool for lamenting thus. Listen:
when impermanence first embraces one who has been born,"
Since she is like a nurse and not one's biological mother, what occasion for grief is there then?
And so it is said:
"Where have those protectors of the earth gone, along with their armies, forces, and vehicles, for whose parting the earth remains even today as a witness? (Hitopadeśa 4.69)
And so it is said:
"For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Whether today or at the end of a hundred years, death is indeed certain for all living beings. (Hitopadeśa 4.70)
Furthermore:
The body is accompanied by imminent ruin; prosperity is the seat of calamities;
meetings end in departures; everything that arises is fragile. (Hitopadeśa 4.71)
This body, wasting away moment by moment, is not perceived; like an unbaked clay jar standing in water, it is only noticed once it has shattered.
Day by day, death draws closer to a living being, just as it approaches step by step a condemned man being led to the place of execution. (Hitopadeśa 4.73)
For it is said:
Youth, beauty, life, the accumulation of wealth, power, and living among loved ones are all impermanent; a wise person would not be deluded by them. (Hitopadeśa 4.74)
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart again—
such is the meeting of living beings.
Just as a certain traveler rests by taking shelter in the shade, and having rested, departs once more—such is the meeting of living beings. (Hitopadeśa 4.76)
And furthermore:

When the body, fashioned from the five elements, has once again returned to the state of the five, and each has reached its own respective source, what cause for lamentation is there? (Hitopadeśa 4.77)
As many dear attachments as a living being forms with the mind, so many spikes of sorrow are driven deep into his heart. (Hitopadeśa 4.78)
This absolute cohabitation cannot be found with anyone, even with one's own body, let alone with any other. (Hitopadeśa 4.79)
Moreover:
For union indeed indicates the impending occurrence of separation, just as the arrival of birth portends the coming of death, which cannot be avoided. (Hitopadeśa 4.80)
For the consequence of unions with loved ones, though delightful at first sight,
is indeed as terrible as that of unwholesome foods.
Moreover:
Just as the currents of rivers flow onward and do not return, so too night and day constantly carry away the lifespan of mortals. (Hitopadeśa 4.82)
But that encounter with the virtuous in saṃsāra which is intent upon the relish of pleasure, because it ends in separation, is yoked to the forefront of sufferings. (Hitopadeśa 4.83)
For this very reason, the virtuous do not desire association with the good, for there is no remedy for a mind severed by the sword of separation from them. (Hitopadeśa 4.84)
Even the meritorious deeds performed by kings such as Sagara and others—
those very deeds have perished, and they too have gone to destruction.
Reflecting again and again upon that Death, who wields a terrible rod over even a wise man,
[all worldly ties] fall away like leather straps soaked by rainwater.
All efforts become slackened. (Hitopadeśa 4.86)
O hero among men, from the very night that beings first enter their dwelling in the womb,
their journey proceeds without faltering.
Day by day, he draws closer to death.
If separation were not the cause, then ignorance would not be the cause;
as the days pass by, why does grief increase rather than depart? (Hitopadeśa 4.88)
Therefore, my good friend, reflect upon yourself and abandon this preoccupation with grief; for—
Of weapons that fall unexpectedly and pierce the vital organs, [there is no remedy].
For those struck by the blows of intense grief, non-reflection alone is the great medicine.
Then, having heard those words, Kauṇḍinya, as if awakened, rose up and said:
"Enough now of dwelling in this hell that is home; I shall go to the forest itself."
Kapila, however, said:
"Even in the forest, faults arise for those possessed by passion; even at home, the restraint of the five senses is asceticism."
He who engages in blameless action, for whom passion has ceased in the three spheres, finds his home to be a grove of asceticism.
For it is said:

"Even if one is suffering, one should practice the Dharma, regardless of which stage of life one is devoted to; being equanimous toward all beings, the external emblem is not the cause of Dharma. (Hitopadeśa 4.91)
And it is said:
"Those for whom eating is for the sake of sustenance, sexual union for the sake of progeny, and speech for the sake of truthful words—they cross over even difficult perils. (Hitopadeśa 4.92)
For it is thus:
the self is a river whose holy fords are self-restraint, whose water is truth, whose banks are virtue, and whose waves are compassion.
Perform your consecration there, O son of Pāṇḍu;
for the inner self does not wither through water alone.
And specifically:
"Happiness belongs to one who abandons this produced, essence-less cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is afflicted by the sufferings of birth, death, old age, and disease. (Hitopadeśa 4.94)
For it is said:

"There is only suffering and no happiness, because that [so-called happiness] is perceived as such; the designation 'happiness' is applied to the remedy for one afflicted by suffering. (Hitopadeśa 4.95)
Kauṇḍinya said, "It was exactly so.
Then I was cursed by that brahmin, who was overwhelmed with grief, saying:
'From this day forward, you shall be the vehicle for frogs.'"
Kapila said: "At present, you are unable to receive instruction;
your heart is overwhelmed by grief.
Nevertheless, hear what must be done."
Attachment should be abandoned with one's whole being; if it cannot be abandoned, it should be directed toward the virtuous, for the company of the virtuous is indeed the remedy.
Furthermore:
Desire should be abandoned by all means; if it cannot be abandoned, it should be directed toward one's own wife, for she alone is its remedy. (Hitopadeśa 4.97)
Having heard this, Kauṇḍinya, the fire of whose grief was extinguished by the nectar of Kapila’s instruction, took up the staff according to the prescribed rite.
Therefore, I remain here to carry frogs because of the Brahmin’s curse.
Immediately thereafter, that frog went and reported this matter before the lord of the frogs, named Jālapāda.
Then that lord of frogs arrived and mounted the back of the serpent;
and the serpent, having placed him upon its back, moved about with a variegated gait.
On the following day, seeing that the lord of frogs was unable to move, he said to him: "Why is your pace so slow today?"
The serpent said, "O King,
I am unable [to move] due to lack of food.
The lord of the frogs replied, "At my command, eat the frogs."
Then, saying, "I have received this great favor," he gradually ate the frogs.
Next, seeing that the pond was devoid of frogs, even the frog-king was eaten by him.
Therefore I say: "One may carry even enemies upon one's shoulder," and so forth.
"Your Majesty, let us now cease this narration of ancient events; in every respect, this King Hiraṇyagarbha must be conciliated—this is my opinion.
The king said, "What is this deliberation of yours?"
Since he has already been defeated by us,
let him remain here if he chooses to stay out of service to us;
otherwise, let him be challenged to battle.
In the meantime, having arrived from Jambūdvīpa, the parrot said:
"Your Majesty, the king of Siṃhaladvīpa, who is a sārasa crane, has now invaded Jambūdvīpa and remains there.
The king asked in great agitation: "What? What?"
The parrot related what had been previously said.
The vulture spoke to himself: "Well done, O minister Cakravāka! Well done!
The king, filled with anger, said: "Let this one be for now; having gone there myself, I shall uproot him along with his very foundation."
The far-sighted one laughed and said:
"One should not engage in vain, thunderous clamor like an autumn cloud; a great man reveals neither the benefit nor the harm of another. (Hitopadeśa 4.98)
Furthermore:
A king should never at one time provoke many who would strike him down;
even a serpent full of pride is surely destroyed by many insects. (Hitopadeśa 4.99)

"O King, how can there be a departure from here without a reconciliation, since he must then direct his wrath against us? Furthermore: He who, without understanding the true nature of the matter, falls under the sway of anger alone..."
That fool, the Brahmin, suffers just as [the mongoose] did from the *nakula*. (4.100)
The king asked, "How was that? Dūradarśin related:
Story 11.
In Ujjayinī there was a Brahmin named Mādhava. His wife, having given birth,
went away to stay elsewhere, leaving the Brahmin behind to look after the protection of the infant child.
Then, an invitation arrived for the Brahmin to receive the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* from the king.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin, due to his innate poverty, thought: "If I do not go quickly, then someone else will hear of it and take the *śrāddha*. For:
When that which is to be received, that which is to be given,
and the duty to be performed are not carried out promptly, time drinks up their essence.
"But there is no protector for this boy here;
what shall I do?
Very well, I shall go, having appointed this mongoose, whom I have nurtured for a long time and who is no different from a son, to guard the boy."
Having done so, he departed.
Then, as he was approaching the boy, that mongoose saw a black cobra; out of anger, he killed it, tore it into pieces, and ate it.
Thereupon, seeing the Brahmin returning, the mongoose—his face and paws smeared with blood—quickly approached and rolled at his feet.
Then that brahmin, seeing him in such a state, concluded, "My child has been eaten by this [creature]," and killed the mongoose.
Immediately after, when the brahmin approached and looked at his offspring, the child was sleeping soundly and the snake lay dead.
Then, observing that helpful mongoose, he—
With his mind thus cultivated, that brahmin fell into extreme despondency;
therefore I say:
"He who, without knowing the true nature of the matter," and so forth. Furthermore—
Lust, anger, greed, exhilaration, pride, and arrogance—one should cast off this group of six; when these are abandoned, O King, one becomes happy.
The king said: "Minister, is this your firm resolve? The minister replied: "It is exactly so; for—"
Mindfulness regarding the objectives, single-minded devotion to them, certainty of knowledge, firmness, and secrecy of counsel are the supreme qualities of a counselor. (Hitopadeśa 4.103)
And so it is said:
One should not perform an action impulsively; lack of discernment is the gateway to supreme calamities.
For prosperity, seeking virtue, chooses of its own accord the man who acts with deliberation.
Therefore, O King, if my words are to be followed now, then let us proceed after making an agreement; for although four means have been taught for accomplishing what is to be achieved:
Their fruit is merely numerical; their accomplishment is established in the Sāman.
The king said, "How can this be expected so soon? The minister replied, "O King, it will happen quickly; for:"
A wicked person is easily broken like a clay pot, yet difficult to repair;
a virtuous person, however, is like a golden vessel.
He is difficult to alienate and quick to reconcile.
An ignorant person is easily pleased, and one who possesses specialized knowledge is even more easily pleased;
however, even Brahmā cannot delight a man who is conceited over a mere fragment of knowledge.
In all cases, the activities of qualities that are beyond perception are to be inferred from their actions;
therefore, one should discern the action of those whose activities are imperceptible by means of their fruits. (Hitopadeśa 4.108)

The king said, "Enough with further debate; let what you intend be carried out. Having deliberated thus, the vulture, the great minister, said, "What is appropriate must be done there," and set out toward the interior of the fortress.
Then, having arrived, the crane Praṇidhi informed Queen Hiraṇyagarbhā: "O Queen, the great minister Vulture is coming to our presence to conclude a peace treaty.
The Royal Swan said: "Minister!"
Furthermore, there was a certain underlying intention for his arrival here.
The Omniscient One smiled and said, "O King,
this is no cause for suspicion."
Since that noble-minded one is far-sighted; or rather, this is the nature of those with dull intellects:
sometimes they do not even entertain a doubt.
Sometimes there is doubt everywhere; for instance,
the swan, deceived by frequently seeing the reflections of stars in the lake, searches for clusters of night-lotuses at night, being unobservant.
Fearing a star, the world does not bite a white lotus even during the day; startled by a mere semblance, people look for danger even where none exists. // Hit_4.109 //
One whose mind has been corrupted by the wicked has no trust even in the virtuous;
a child who has been burned by milk-rice eats even curd only after blowing upon it. (Hitopadeśa 4.110)
"Therefore, Your Majesty, let the necessary materials for that worship, such as offerings of jewels and the like, be prepared according to our capacity.

When this had been done, the vulture was approached by the cakravāka at the gate of the fortress; having been honored and brought inside, he was granted an audience with the king and sat down upon the seat provided.
The Cakravāka said: "O Minister, everything depends on you; let this kingdom be enjoyed according to your own will.
The Rājahaṃsa replied: "Just so."
Dūradarśin said: "It is exactly so; however, further elaborate speech is now useless. For it is said:
'One should win over the greedy with wealth, and the arrogant by joining one's palms in reverence.'"
One should treat a fool according to his whims, but a wise man according to the truth.
Furthermore:
One should win over a friend through sincerity, kinsmen through respectful attentiveness, a wife and servants through gifts and honors, and other people through courtesy. (Hitopadeśa 4.112)
"Therefore, let us go now to reconcile with King Citravarṇa, who possesses great majesty. The Cakravāka said, "Let it be done in such a way that peace is established."
"Let that also be told.
The royal swan said: "How many types of treaties are possible?
The vulture replied: "I shall tell you; listen."
But a king who is attacked by one more powerful and has no other remedy, having fallen into calamity, should seek a treaty while biding his time. (Hitopadeśa 4.113)
The skull, the offering, the lineage, the association, the proposal, the remedy, the union, and the intervention of another person. (Hitopadeśa 4.114)
The unseen man, the instructed one, the capture for the sake of self-flesh, the ransom, the severed one, and likewise the defiler of others. (Hitopadeśa 4.115)
"The junction brought about by the aggregates is proclaimed as the sixteenth;
thus those skilled in junctions declare the junction to be sixteenfold. (Hitopadeśa 4.116)
The joint of the skull should be known as consisting solely of a flat joint;
that which arises from the act of giving is called an offering. (Hitopadeśa 4.117)
The continuity of the lineage should be understood as being preceded by the giving of a daughter;
however, the alliance formed with the virtuous is said to be preceded by loving-kindness. (Hitopadeśa 4.118)
But he who, for as long as his lifespan lasts, shares the same purpose and aim, and who is not divided by any circumstances—whether in prosperity or in adversity—is a true friend. (Hitopadeśa 4.119)
This alliance is indeed a union that, due to its excellence, is like gold;
thus it has been described as "golden" by others skilled in diplomacy. (Hitopadeśa 4.120)
That which is performed with the aim of accomplishing one's own purpose is called an "upanyāsa" by those skilled in such strategic propositions. (Hitopadeśa 4.121)
"I have previously rendered assistance to him; he too will do so for me"—an alliance formed on this basis is called a reciprocal alliance. (Hitopadeśa 4.122)
"I shall do him a favor, and he will do one for me; this is a reciprocal service, like that between Rāma and Sugrīva. (Hitopadeśa 4.123)
When two parties proceed on a journey toward a single objective with a perfectly coordinated advance, that alliance is called *saṃyoga*. (Hitopadeśa 4.124)
"Let my purpose be accomplished by the two chief warriors among us"—when such a wager is made, that peace is one mediated through another person. (Hitopadeśa 4.125)
"‘This objective of mine must be accomplished by you alone’—where an enemy makes such a wager, that is known as an *adṛṣṭapuruṣa* (the unseen man). (Hitopadeśa 4.126)

When a powerful enemy is made to enter into peace by those skilled in treaties on the condition of surrendering a portion of his territory as tribute, that is declared and designated as *ādiṣṭa* (the stipulated peace).
Making peace with one's own army when one is threatened by oneself is declared [as the best course];
it is undertaken for the sake of protecting one's life, being superior to the giving away of everything. (Hitopadeśa 4.128)
Whether by a portion of one's treasury, half the treasury, or even the entire treasury, the purchase [of the Dharma] is prescribed for the sake of protecting what remains. (Hitopadeśa 4.129)
By the gift of fertile lands, one is said to be "one who has cut through [poverty]," and by the gift of all the fruits arising from the earth, one becomes the ornament of others. (Hitopadeśa 4.130)

Where a limited fruit is bestowed by each individual aggregate (skandha), those skilled in the nature of junctions call that a "junction" (sandhi) which is brought about by the aggregates. (Hitopadeśa 4.131)
Mutual assistance, friendship, kinship, and tribute—these four should be understood as the types of alliances. (Hitopadeśa 4.132)
Indeed, it is our view that there is only one form of conciliation, namely *upahāra* (bribery);
all other varieties, with the exception of *maitra* (friendship), are merely different forms of *upahāra*. (Hitopadeśa 4.133)
Since an aggressor who possesses superior force does not desist without having achieved his objective, no other form of peace exists for him except through the payment of tribute. (Hitopadeśa 4.134)
The king said, "Gentlemen, you are great and wise;
therefore, please instruct us on what must be done in this matter.
Dūradarśin replied, "Ah! Why do you speak thus?"

For what person indeed would practice that which is devoid of Dharma for the sake of this body, which is overcome by mental and physical afflictions and destined to perish today or tomorrow? (Hitopadeśa 4.135)
The life of embodied beings is indeed as flickering as the moon reflected in water;
knowing it to be such, one should constantly practice what is wholesome. (Hitopadeśa 4.136)
This sovereignty over the earth is as fleeting as a cloud driven by the wind;
the enjoyment of sensory objects is sweet only for a moment;
and life is as unstable as a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass.
Dharma is indeed the supreme companion on the journey to the next world.
Having perceived that saṃsāra is like a mirage and momentary in its destruction, one should associate with virtuous people for the sake of the Dharma and for happiness. (Hitopadeśa 4.138)
Therefore, let that very thing be done according to my approval; for— A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held upon a scale.
Indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices. (Hitopadeśa 4.139)
"Therefore, let a peace treaty named 'Golden' be established between these two kings, preceded by an ordeal of speaking the truth.
Sarvajña said, "So be it.
Then King Rājahaṃsa honored the minister Dūradarśin with gifts of garments and ornaments.
With a joyful mind, he took the cakravāka bird and went into the presence of King Mayūra.
There, King Citravarṇa, following the words of the vulture, spoke to Sarvajña with great honor and gifts; having accepted such a treaty, Sarvajña was dispatched to the vicinity of the royal swan.
Dūradarśī said:
"O King, our desired goal is accomplished; now let us return, turning back toward our own abode on Mount Vindhya."
Then, having all reached their own places, they obtained the fruits they had desired. Viṣṇuśarman said: "What else shall I tell you?"
"Let it be said.
The princes replied, "Noble sir,
through your grace, the entire administration of the kingdom has been established."
"Therefore, we have become happy.
Viṣṇuśarman said: "Even if this is so, let there also be this other [blessing]:
May there always be peace for all victorious kings, and may there be constant joy."
May the virtuous be free from calamity, and may the fame of those who perform good deeds increase for a long time.
May the goddess of policy, like a courtesan, remain ever upon the chest of ministers and kiss their faces; may there be a great festival every single day. (Hitopadeśa 4.140)
And let there be something else as well:
as long as the moon-crested Lord remains the abode of the love of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain,
and as long as Lakṣmī flashes in the mind of Murāri like lightning in a cloud;
As long as this Golden Mountain stands, equal to a forest fire with the sun as its sparks, so long may this collection of stories composed by Nārāyaṇa continue to circulate. (Hitopadeśa 4.141)
Furthermore:
May Indra bestow desired rain, causing the earth to produce abundant crops; may the foremost of Brahmins duly perform the gratification of the gods with their favorite offerings;

may the fellowship of the virtuous remain firm and well-nourished until the end of the aeon; and may the unbearable words of malicious people, like adamantine glue, come to a complete and total peace. (Hitopadeśa 4.142)
Furthermore:
May that illustrious Dhavalacandra, the regional ruler, triumph over his enemies—he by whom this compendium was diligently caused to be written and circulated. (Hitopadeśa 4.143)
Thus ends the fourth collection of stories, named "Peace," in the *Hitopadeśa*.
And this *Hitopadeśa* is completed.
